name: Incidental liver mass
lead: Whether this lesion needs anything at all, which single test will say so, and — if it is not benign — which disease pathway the patient belongs on, named, before anyone passes a needle.
gatelabel: The decision in front of you

gates.name: 0 · Is this an at-risk liver?
crit: Cirrhosis of any aetiology
Chronic hepatitis B infection, with or without cirrhosis
Current or prior hepatocellular carcinoma, including a liver transplant candidate or recipient
None of the above — a liver with no risk factor for primary liver cancer
A vascular liver disorder, congenital hepatic fibrosis, or age under 18 — a separate category in which LI-RADS does not apply at all
gates.ask: Before I order anything else: is this liver in the population whose imaging criteria are allowed to make a diagnosis?

standard.t: Answer the at-risk question first, because it decides which diagnostic criteria you are permitted to use for the rest of the workup.
standard.pref: Every incidental liver lesion, before the next scan is ordered. The LI-RADS at-risk population is cirrhosis, chronic hepatitis B, and current or prior HCC including adult transplant candidates. AASLD 2023 and EASL 2025 both build their diagnostic algorithms on that same population and both use the LI-RADS lexicon; EASL 2025 states that LI-RADS should be preferred over its own 2018 algorithm because of the LR-M and LR-TIV categories, while noting the two perform similarly for HCC (LoE 3, strong recommendation).
standard.avoid: Do not let the referral's wording settle this. 'Known liver disease' on a request form is not the same as cirrhosis, and MASLD without cirrhosis is not an at-risk liver under either guideline.
standard.note: Record the aetiology and how cirrhosis was established — histology, imaging, elastography, platelet count, or clinical decompensation. The at-risk answer is the single most consequential line in the report.

standard.t: In an at-risk liver, categorise the observation with CT/MRI LI-RADS v2018 and put the category in the report — but read the category as a probability derived from retrospective high-prevalence cohorts, not as a measurement.
standard.pref: Every observation in an at-risk liver. In a systematic review of 17 retrospective studies, 2,760 patients and 3,556 observations, the pooled proportions confirmed as HCC and as any malignancy were 94% (95% CI 92-96) and 97% (95-99) for LR-5, 74% (67-80) and 80% (75-85) for LR-4, 38% (31-45) and 40% (31-50) for LR-3, 13% (8-22) and 14% (9-21) for LR-2, and 36% (26-48) and 93% (87-97) for LR-M; no malignancy was found in LR-1.
standard.avoid: Three things undercut those figures. All 17 studies were retrospective and observation selection was the commonest high-risk domain, through verification bias and case-control design, so the LR-3 and LR-4 figures are probably inflated relative to an unselected incidental population; the authors themselves call the LR-2 estimate provisional and at high risk of bias while still recommending that LR-2 management be reconsidered, and this page does not inherit that recommendation. The 2022 individual-patient-data meta-analysis of 5,364 observations from 32 studies then shows the major features are not equivalent: nonperipheral washout carried an odds ratio of 13.2 (95% CI 9.0-19.2) and nonrim arterial hyperenhancement 10.3 (6.7-15.6), enhancing capsule only 2.4 (1.7-3.5), and threshold growth was not associated with HCC at all, OR 1.6 (0.8-3.4) — a result the same paper reports a second time as 1.6 (0.7-3.6), p=0.07.
standard.note: The agreement figures matter as much as the probabilities. Interreader agreement for arterial hyperenhancement and washout is excellent, kappa 0.84-0.87, but agreement on the category that actually drives management is fair for CEUS (kappa 0.30-0.39), fair to substantial for MRI (0.35-0.61) and substantial for CT (0.79), and intermodality agreement is kappa 0.33-0.39 between CT and MRI and 0.22 between MRI and CEUS. A category is not a stable property of the lesion. See the quick reference for the v2018 table.

standard.t: In a liver that is not at risk, accept that no imaging criterion set exists that can call a lesion hepatocellular carcinoma — EASL 2025 says so explicitly, and the consequence is that an unresolved solid lesion here needs tissue, not another category.
standard.pref: The young patient, the patient with no liver disease, and the patient with MASLD and no cirrhosis. EASL 2025: the non-invasive criteria should only be applied to patients with cirrhosis, chronic HBV infection or a history of HCC, and in other patients the diagnosis of HCC should be confirmed by biopsy (LoE 1, strong recommendation). The guideline gives its own reason — the pre-test probability in these populations has not been precisely established.
standard.avoid: Do not apply a LI-RADS category outside the at-risk population and then act on it. The number means nothing there, and it will be read as though it did.
standard.note: This does not mean every solid lesion in a normal liver needs a needle. Most are haemangioma, focal fat or focal nodular hyperplasia and are resolved on this page at gates 4 and 5. It means that an unresolved solid lesion in a normal liver cannot be declared malignant or benign by imaging category alone.

alt.t: Where cirrhosis is suspected but not established, say so in those words and treat the pathway as undetermined rather than guessing in either direction.
alt.pref: Advanced fibrosis on elastography without decompensation, a nodular liver contour without portal hypertension, long-standing alcohol use with normal synthetic function. Name the uncertainty, get the hepatology opinion, and decide the pathway once.
alt.avoid: Do not default to the at-risk pathway because it feels safer. It is not neutral: it licenses a treat-without-tissue decision for LR-5, and in a non-cirrhotic liver that decision has no evidence behind it.

alt.t: In a liver with a vascular disorder — Budd-Chiari, chronic portal vein occlusion, obliterative portal venopathy, hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia, cardiac congestion — treat the case as its own category and get it to a benign-liver-tumour multidisciplinary review rather than through either arm of this gate.
alt.pref: These livers generate multiple arterially hyperenhancing benign nodules — in Budd-Chiari syndrome, imaging displays hepatic nodules in 60-80% of patients, usually under 4 cm, frequently more than ten, hypervascular and disseminated, with no pathognomonic CT or MRI pattern — and LI-RADS specifically excludes cirrhosis caused by vascular disorders and by congenital hepatic fibrosis from its population. EASL's vascular-liver-disease guideline is the document that governs them, and it states plainly that characterisation of these nodules cannot rely on the HCC criteria validated in cirrhosis.
alt.avoid: Do not categorise a hyperenhancing nodule in a Budd-Chiari liver as LR-4 or LR-5 and act on it, and do not treat benignity as settled either: cumulative HCC incidence in Budd-Chiari syndrome is about 4% at a median 5 years. Note what the guideline does not give you — it reports how often these nodules occur in patients known to have vascular disease, and never the inverse probability a radiologist actually faces, which is the chance of underlying vascular disease given multiple hypervascular nodules in a non-cirrhotic liver. The five biopsy triggers it suggests (three or fewer nodules, a nodule 3 cm or larger, heterogeneity or venous-phase washout, change across two studies, rising alpha-fetoprotein) come from one cited source with no sensitivity or specificity, in the same paragraph that says the only formal recommendation is multidisciplinary surveillance.
alt.note: Two provenance warnings. First, the EASL vascular-liver guidance this page quotes is the 2015 document, built on the agenda of a single 2012 conference with a PubMed-only search and committee opinion where evidence was absent; it has been superseded by a 2026 EASL edition that this page has not obtained, so every statement sourced to it here is provisional and must be re-checked against the new edition before clinical use. Second, the entity the 2015 guideline calls idiopathic non-cirrhotic portal hypertension has been redefined by the 2026 multisociety consensus as porto-sinusoidal vascular disorder or non-cirrhotic portal fibrosis, and nodular regenerative hyperplasia is now a major histological criterion for that disorder rather than a benign nodular tumour to reassure a patient about. Grade D on purpose: this is a scope rule drawn from documents that grade their own evidence as committee opinion.

avoid.t: Do not use a LI-RADS category outside the at-risk population, and do not write one into a report for a patient who has no risk factor.
avoid.pref: Describe the findings in the lexicon — arterial hyperenhancement, washout, capsule — without assigning a category, and route by what the lesion looks like.
avoid.avoid: A category assigned outside its population is the commonest way a benign adenoma or a metastasis gets treated as HCC.

avoid.t: Do not start a workup before the chart has been read.
avoid.pref: Risk factors for chronic liver disease, prior cancer, oestrogen and androgen exposure, metabolic syndrome, foreign travel and dysentery, constitutional symptoms, and baseline liver tests all change the differential before any scan is added. EASL's benign-tumour guideline puts the history and the baseline bloods ahead of the contrast study for exactly this reason.
avoid.avoid: Ordering the next scan without the history is how a patient ends up with three studies and no diagnosis.

gates.name: 1 · Known extrahepatic malignancy?
crit: An active or previously treated extrahepatic primary with a propensity to metastasise to the liver
Colorectal, breast, lung, pancreatic, gastro-oesophageal, neuroendocrine, melanoma, sarcoma or renal primary
On, or recently off, systemic therapy — which changes both the parenchyma and the appearance of the lesion
No known primary — in which case the pre-test probability of malignancy in a small lesion is close to nil
gates.ask: Does this patient have a primary that explains the lesion, and does that primary have a pathway page of its own?

standard.t: Characterise with MRI, including diffusion-weighted imaging, rather than repeating the CT — but order it for the sub-centimetre lesion, which is the only place MRI has been shown to beat CT.
standard.pref: Any indeterminate lesion in a patient with a known extrahepatic malignancy. The ACR incidental-findings algorithm names MRI as the modality for further workup in all four of its core recommendations, and the ACR Appropriateness Criteria make MRI without and with intravenous contrast the only option rated usually appropriate for a sub-centimetre lesion found on ultrasound in a patient with a known extrahepatic malignancy.
standard.avoid: Do not overstate the margin. In a meta-analysis of 39 prospective studies and 3,391 untreated colorectal cancer patients, per-lesion sensitivity was 80.3% (95% CI 74.6-85.0) for MRI against 74.4% (68.7-79.3) for CT — overlapping intervals, no significant difference — and per-patient sensitivity 88.2% (64.8-96.8) against 83.6% (66.9-92.8), p=0.653, also not significant. The one real advantage is below 10 mm: 60.2% (54.4-65.7) for MRI against 47.3% (40.1-54.5) for CT, p=0.006. At 10 mm or larger there is no difference at all, 89.0% against 86.7%, p=0.617. Note also what the meta-analysis did not find: liver-specific contrast material, multisection scanners and dual-phase acquisition each gave no measurable benefit, so the case for MRI rests on the sequences and not on the agent.
standard.note: Two cautions on transporting those numbers. They come from treatment-naive patients being staged for a known colorectal primary, where prevalence is high; the paper reports no predictive values at all, and after chemotherapy steatosis and sinusoidal injury degrade detection on every modality. And the figure that matters for a sub-centimetre lesion cuts against reassurance: the test being ordered to characterise it misses two metastases in five at that size. The same paper publishes two incompatible sets of per-patient sensitivities — 83.6, 88.2 and 94.1% in the abstract and Table 4, and 81.2, 93.4 and 94.2% in its own summary box — and does not reconcile them.

standard.t: Treat a sub-centimetre lesion in a cancer patient as probably benign but explicitly unresolved, and say which of the two it is in the report.
standard.pref: Every small lesion reported in a patient under oncological surveillance. In 2,978 cancer patients who had both an initial and a follow-up abdominal CT at one cancer centre, a small hepatic lesion was mentioned in the radiology report of 378 (12.7%); 44 of the 378 (11.6%) grew and were counted metastatic, 303 (80.2%) were stable over a mean 25.6 months, and 31 (8.2%) were stable for under 6 months and left indeterminate. The rate varied by primary: metastatic in 3 of 76 (4%) with lymphoma, 8 of 57 (14%) with colorectal cancer and 14 of 63 (22%) with breast cancer.
standard.avoid: Do not quote 11.6% as the malignant rate without saying it is the most favourable of three analyses the authors ran. Counting all 31 indeterminates as malignant gives 19.8%, and splitting them evenly gives 15.7% — nearly one in five at the top end. Benignity was defined as not growing on the same test, with no histology in any case, and requiring a second CT at the same institution conditions the cohort on surviving and staying in follow-up, which preferentially removes the patients whose lesions would have grown. The ACR algorithm's rule for this patient is a new sub-centimetre lesion in a high-risk liver gets MRI at 3 to 6 months — a deliberate interval, not a discharge.
standard.note: Number and size pull in different directions in the two series and neither is decisive. In the cancer-centre cohort, solitary and multiple lesions did not differ significantly (metastatic in 9.8% against 14.0%, p>0.05), and nor did the presence of extrahepatic metastases (36% against 25.7%, p>0.05); the study was underpowered for both and reports no power calculation. In the older 1,454-examination CT series, the gradient by number was steep — 5% of patients with one small lesion progressed against 76% of those with five or more — but lesion number there is confounded with tumour burden and stage.

standard.t: Route by the primary's name, not by the word metastasis: a known colorectal primary is the CRLM pathway from here, and a known neuroendocrine primary is the NELM pathway from here.
standard.pref: As soon as the primary is established. Those pathways carry their own resectability, sequencing and biopsy rules, and the most common way to damage a patient at this gate is to start a generic workup instead of entering the right pathway. For colorectal disease in particular the consequence is concrete — biopsy of a resectable colorectal liver metastasis is contraindicated on that pathway, and this page's job is to get the patient there before anyone books one.
standard.avoid: Do not route on an assumption. A liver lesion in a patient with a treated colorectal cancer is not automatically a colorectal metastasis, and the local master workup CPG requires colorectal origin to be confirmed and the primary's status verified before the CRLM pathway is entered.
standard.note: The local Master Workup and Staging CPG sets the minimum staging bundle for each destination: CT or MRI of chest, abdomen and pelvis plus FDG PET-CT, CEA, colonoscopy and molecular profile for CRLM; somatostatin-receptor imaging, cross-sectional staging and central review of grade and Ki-67 for neuroendocrine liver metastases.

opts.name: FDG PET-CT
opts.when: The ACR Appropriateness Criteria rate FDG PET-CT usually appropriate in exactly one of eight variants — an indeterminate liver lesion larger than 1 cm found on non-contrast or single-phase CT or non-contrast MRI in a patient with a known extrahepatic malignancy. For the same lesion found on ultrasound it drops to may be appropriate, and it is rated usually not appropriate in a normal liver on the explicit basis that there is no relevant literature supporting its use there.
opts.pref: The larger indeterminate lesion where the question is whether disease is confined to the liver, since the test answers a staging question the liver MRI cannot. Per-patient sensitivity for colorectal liver metastases was 94.1% (95% CI 91.6-95.9), higher than CT at 83.6% (66.9-92.8), p=0.025.
opts.avoid: Do not use it to clear a small lesion. Per-lesion sensitivity was 81.4% (66.5-90.6), statistically indistinguishable from MRI at 80.3%, and the FDG PET/CT data specifically amounted to one per-lesion data set, far too few for comparison with other modalities. A negative PET does not characterise a sub-centimetre lesion.

opts.name: Somatostatin-receptor PET
opts.when: The functional study for a suspected or known neuroendocrine primary, and the one the local master workup CPG names in the minimum staging bundle for neuroendocrine liver metastases. The ACR Appropriateness Criteria rate DOTATATE PET-CT may be appropriate for an indeterminate lesion larger than 1 cm in a patient with a known extrahepatic malignancy, and usually not appropriate in a normal liver.
opts.pref: A hypervascular, often multiple lesion set in a patient with flushing, diarrhoea, a known small-bowel or pancreatic primary, or a previously resected neuroendocrine tumour — which is the NELM pathway from here.
opts.avoid: Do not substitute it for cross-sectional liver imaging; it answers receptor status and whole-body distribution, not resectability. And do not read the appropriateness rating as evidence — the criteria dismiss it in the normal-liver variants on the stated ground that no relevant literature exists, which is absence of evidence converted into a numerical rating.

alt.order: Ordered by how often each is the right answer in an unselected incidental population, not by any comparative trial — none compares them for this indication. Both are second tests ordered for a named reason; neither characterises a lesion the liver MRI left indeterminate.
alt.flagnote: Ratification item: whether FDG PET-CT may be ordered from the radiology report alone for an indeterminate lesion in a cancer patient, or only after the primary team has named the question. The ACR criteria support the test in one narrow variant and the commonest local failure is ordering it in the other seven — but note that those ratings are panel medians from a RAND/UCLA process whose rating dispersion and evidence grading are published on a separate ACR website and not in the paper, so the group cannot tell from the publication which ratings were near-unanimous and which were marginal. Audit: PET-CT ordered for liver characterisation, by lesion size and risk category.

alt.t: Where the lesion is the only evidence of metastatic disease and would change the treatment plan from curative to palliative, treat that as a multidisciplinary question rather than a radiological one.
alt.pref: The patient about to have a curative resection of a colorectal, breast or lung primary, in whom one sub-centimetre liver lesion appeared on the staging CT. The 80.2% stability rate in the 2,978-patient series is a reason to re-image rather than to abandon the operation — bearing in mind that the same series puts the malignant rate anywhere from 11.6% to 19.8% depending on how its 31 indeterminate lesions are counted.
alt.avoid: Do not let an 8 mm indeterminate lesion cancel a curative operation without the board seeing it, and do not let it be ignored either.

avoid.t: Do not biopsy a liver lesion in a patient whose colorectal liver metastases are resectable.
avoid.pref: Confirm colorectal origin from the primary's pathology and operate. This is the position of the CRLM pathway and the reason routing by name matters at this gate.
avoid.avoid: In 598 patients resected with curative intent for colorectal metastases, 90 had been biopsied before referral and 17 of those 90 (19%) had needle-track deposits; 4-year overall survival after resection was 32.5% (standard error 5.5) against 46.7% (2.8) in the 508 not biopsied, p=0.008, an absolute difference of 14.2% (95% CI 2.0-26.4). Read the limits honestly, because they are larger than the paper admits. Every biopsy happened at a referring hospital, so the exposure is really a referral route and a marker of diagnostic uncertainty; the biopsied group had synchronous colorectal and hepatic disease in 61% against 26%, p<0.001, the single largest prognostic imbalance in the paper, dismissed without any multivariable model; the claimed independent effect of biopsy is reported as 'p=0.001, Student's t test' with no hazard ratio, confidence interval or covariate list; and conditioning the denominator on having reached a curative resection removes the patients whom dissemination had already made inoperable. The 19% track-deposit rate is the harder number, though open biopsy at laparotomy produced as many deposits as a percutaneous needle (22% against 15%, p=0.398), which suggests some of what was counted is laparotomy implantation rather than needle tracking.
avoid.note: The counterweight is real and also thin: in the same series, inadvertent resection for benign disease without preoperative histology occurred in 6 of 514 (1.2%) — two haemangiomas and four cysts — in a specialist unit with intraoperative ultrasound. Six events in expert hands is not a rate that transports to a general surgical setting.

avoid.t: Do not characterise a liver lesion on a scan that was not acquired to characterise it.
avoid.pref: If the study was a single-phase staging CT, say the lesion is unresolved and name the test that would resolve it.
avoid.avoid: The ACR algorithm's benign and suspicious feature lists assume adequate phases and adequate dose; it warns that assessing small liver lesions is challenging when aggressive dose-reduction has been used, particularly in high-risk patients.

gates.name: 2 · The cystic lesion — resolved here or escalated here
crit: Homogeneous water attenuation, roughly −10 to +20 HU, sharply marginated, no wall thickening, no septation, no mural nodule, no enhancement
Multiple sub-15 mm cystic foci scattered through both lobes, no biliary communication on MRCP — biliary hamartomas
Fever, rigors, raised inflammatory markers, a rim-enhancing collection with surrounding oedema — abscess
Any septation, mural nodularity, wall thickening, enhancing component, or a daughter-cyst or membrane pattern — not a simple cyst
Measured enhancement greater than 20 HU between pre- and post-contrast phases, with pseudoenhancement excluded
gates.ask: Is this water in a bag, or is it something that needs an operation or a drain?

standard.t: A homogeneous, sharply marginated, non-enhancing lesion of water attenuation is a simple cyst: say so, give no follow-up interval, and discharge it.
standard.pref: The commonest cystic finding by a wide margin. The ACR criteria are -10 to +20 Hounsfield units, homogeneous and sharply marginated, with no enhancement, wall thickening, nodularity or septa; enhancement should be 20 HU or less after contrast. In 45,319 ultrasound examinations at one German university hospital, hepatic cysts were the second commonest of five pre-specified benign findings at 2,631 (5.81%), mean size 22.3 mm, solitary in 62.8%, rising monotonically with age from 0.8% in those under 30.
standard.avoid: Three cautions, two of them the white paper's own. Pseudoenhancement can make a genuinely benign cyst measure above 20 HU, so a single high reading is not proof of a solid component — and the same document concedes that in a lesion under 1 cm an accurate density measurement may not be attainable at all, which is precisely where most of the caseload sits. Cystic metastases exist, with ovarian cancer and gastrointestinal stromal tumours the named examples, so low density alone is not definitive in a patient with cancer. And the 5.81% figure is a prevalence of one benign finding in a hospital ultrasound population, not a probability that this cyst is benign: metastases, HCC, abscess and biliary hamartoma were never counted in that study's numerator.
standard.note: Discharge rule: a simple cyst in a patient with no known malignancy needs no imaging follow-up, no size threshold and no interval. Symptoms from a large cyst are a surgical question, not a diagnostic one. The 20 HU threshold itself is a consensus number — the 2010 white paper gave it as 'up to about 20 HU' and invoked radiologists' discretion to resolve the pseudoenhancement problem — so it is a reporting convention, not a derived cut-point.

standard.t: Multiple small non-enhancing cystic foci that do not communicate with the biliary tree on MRCP are biliary hamartomas — von Meyenburg complexes — and the diagnosis is made on MRI, not by counting them on CT.
standard.pref: The patient whose CT was read as multiple sub-centimetre hypodensities, which is the point at which a cancer patient gets labelled metastatic by mistake. These are ductal plate malformations, usually 1 to 15 mm and mostly under 5 mm, subcapsular and periportal, and they are common: a single autopsy series of 2,843 cases gives a prevalence of about 5.6%, and in 95 forensic autopsies of men aged 35 to 69 with targeted sectioning, bile duct tumours were the most frequent finding at 26 cases (27%), mean diameter 1.3 mm, multiple in 46% of the men.
standard.avoid: The published difficulty is exactly the one that matters here. The review states that on CT these lesions cannot be distinguished from small metastases in a patient with a known primary, and that ultrasound is non-specific. It then recommends heavily T2-weighted MRI with MR cholangiography as the discriminator without reporting a single sensitivity, specificity or predictive value for any of those features, and concedes that fibrous-predominant complexes may not be visible on MRI at all. If the clinical setting is a known primary and the foci are not uniform, resolve it on MRI and accept that the resolution is a judgement, not a measurement.
standard.note: Grade D, downgraded from C after the full-text read: the entire imaging recommendation rests on a narrative single-centre review with no search strategy, no accuracy data and no interobserver agreement, and the autopsy prevalence is one secondhand figure from one 1996 series. Discharge rule with a caveat: no surveillance interval is established, and the pathway discharges them. About 35 cases of cholangiocarcinoma arising in von Meyenburg complexes have been reported in roughly fifty years, against a carrier prevalence of about 5.6% — so the absolute risk is vanishingly small and has never been computed. See the honest section.

standard.t: A rim-enhancing collection in a febrile patient is an abscess until proved otherwise: take cultures, start antibiotics, and drain it with a catheter rather than a needle.
standard.pref: Fever, rigors, right upper quadrant pain and a raised white count with a cystic-looking lesion. In a meta-analysis of 12 randomised trials and 1,425 adults, percutaneous catheter drainage gave a higher clinical success rate than percutaneous needle aspiration, odds ratio 4.12 (95% CI 2.01-8.45), p<0.001.
standard.avoid: Carry four limits with that odds ratio. The abscess size subgroup that matters most is the one that fails: in the 5-10 cm stratum, which is 8 of the 12 trials and the commonest clinical scenario, the confidence interval crossed the line of no effect, and only the >5 cm and >10 cm strata — three trials between them — excluded it; the paper's abstract nonetheless reports that the subgroups 'confirmed the consistency of this benefit', which is true of the direction of point estimates and not of significance. Nine of the 12 trials were Indian and 8 enrolled mixed amoebic-predominant abscesses, so pyogenic abscess is represented by 3 trials and 212 patients with no pyogenic-only pooled estimate reported. 'Clinical treatment success' is never defined, and the authors name varying definitions as a likely source of the 56% heterogeneity, so the pooled effect is an odds ratio on an undefined composite. And the safety claim is not equivalence: the complication odds ratio of 1.02 comes from 7 of the 12 trials with a 95% interval of 0.30-3.50, which permits a 70% reduction or a 3.5-fold increase.
standard.note: Treat the odds ratio as a direction, not a threshold, and note that the pooled comparison does not identify a size below which a single aspiration is sufficient. A necrotic metastasis and a necrotic cholangiocarcinoma can both look like an abscess, and an abscess can be the first sign of an occult cancer — see the alternative column. The ACR incidental-findings algorithm explicitly does not cover hepatic infection, so nothing on this gate comes from it.

alt.t: After a pyogenic liver abscess with no obvious source, investigate for an occult cancer rather than treating the abscess as the whole diagnosis.
alt.pref: Every cryptogenic pyogenic abscess, and particularly a diabetic patient. In a Taiwanese claims cohort of 1,257 patients with ICD-coded pyogenic liver abscess and no prior cancer, followed a median 3.33 years, the standardised incidence ratio against national rates was 3.83 (95% CI 3.30-4.42) for all cancers, 7.87 (5.94-10.21) for liver cancer, 34.58 (21.67-52.36) for biliary tract cancer and 5.27 (3.76-7.18) for colorectal cancer.
alt.avoid: Read the time course and the denominator before acting on those ratios. The highest ratios all fell in the first 90 days to one year — all cancers 360.82 (278.46-459.91), biliary tract 1,153 (694-1,801) — which cannot be a biological effect of an abscess; it is the result of imaging and endoscoping a patient intensively, and in some cases the cancer caused the abscess or was the abscess. Several of those ratios are built on expected counts of 0.01 to 0.02 cases and are numerically meaningless however many decimal places they carry. The comparison is to the general Taiwanese population adjusted for age and sex only, in a cohort that was 47.6% diabetic and 7.8% cirrhotic; cirrhosis alone moves the liver-cancer ratio from 4.21 to 59.77, so the unstratified 7.87 is a confounded average, and no matched internal comparator was constructed although the same database could have supplied one. Exposure is two or more appearances of one ICD-9 code with no imaging, culture or clinical validation. The only estimate consistent with a genuine late effect is the all-cancer ratio beyond 5 years, 1.52 (1.09-2.05).
alt.note: The practical inference is to complete the search now, not to enrol the patient in long-term surveillance — and the inference runs the opposite way from how this cohort is usually cited: it is evidence that a lesion called an abscess may be a cancer, not that an abscess will become one. What 'the search' consists of is a local decision: cross-sectional imaging is already done, and the cohort gives no yield estimate, no modality and no stratification, so whether every cryptogenic abscess gets a colonoscopy is not settled by it.

alt.t: A cystic lesion with septations, mural nodularity or an enhancing component is a surgical lesion — get it to MRI and to a hepatobiliary surgeon, and plan for resection rather than drainage.
alt.pref: The multilocular cyst, the cyst with an internal nodule, the cyst that has grown. Mucinous cystic neoplasm of the liver is the entity being excluded, it carries malignant potential, and the operation is complete resection with negative margins.
alt.avoid: Do not aspirate or fenestrate it. The published series are small, selected and worse than they first appear — in one report of six resected intrahepatic biliary cystadenomas from a single Karachi pathology file over seven years, every case had been operated on under a preoperative impression of simple or hydatid cyst, sizes ranged 5.5 to 14.0 cm, and recurrence occurred in three of the five patients in whom any follow-up was available, two patients having been lost, one of them after a recurrence was already documented. Margins could not be assessed in at least three of the six because the specimens arrived opened or in pieces, so the claim that recurrence follows incomplete excision is inferred rather than shown; no dysplasia or malignancy was found in any of the six, and the 20% malignant-transformation figure the series invokes to justify radical resection is a single citation with no denominator. The authors attribute their own recurrence rate partly to limited local hepatobiliary surgical expertise. Six cases is not an evidence base; it is a warning about what the misdiagnosis costs.
alt.note: Grade D on purpose. There is no comparative evidence for resection over observation in a radiologically suspected mucinous cystic neoplasm, no study establishes how often a septated cystic liver lesion is one, and the septation sign itself is contradicted by the series' own figure legend, which records one case as having no internal septations and reads that as favouring cystadenoma.

alt.t: Where the history includes relevant exposure, consider cystic echinococcosis and stage it on imaging before touching it.
alt.pref: Foreign travel or residence in an endemic area, sheep or dog contact, a cyst with daughter cysts, detached membranes or a calcified wall. The WHO Informal Working Group on Echinococcosis consensus is an image-based, stage-specific approach grouping cysts as active (CE1, CE2), transitional (CE3) and inactive (CE4, CE5), and it recommends strongly that an imaging-based classification system be used; the four options it sets out are percutaneous treatment, surgery, anti-infective drug treatment, or watch and wait. Puncture, aspiration, injection and re-aspiration with mandatory albendazole cover is first-line for CE1 and CE3a cysts larger than 5 cm, and is contraindicated for CE2, CE3b, CE4 and CE5.
alt.avoid: Do not aspirate a suspected hydatid cyst as though it were a simple cyst or an abscess, and do not treat an unclassified cyst at all until its parasitic nature is proven. The stage decides the option, and the stage is a subjective ultrasound judgement for which the consensus reports no interobserver agreement, while noting that calcification — the most objective feature — is unreliable for viability and occurs at every stage. The consensus states that percutaneous treatment should only be undertaken by experienced operators with resuscitation drugs and a surgical back-up team, but never states an anaphylaxis rate, and gives no sensitivity or specificity for any test in the document, including the two sequential serological assays it requires.
alt.note: Grade D, downgraded from C after the full-text read. Ten of the eleven graded recommendations in this consensus are Strength B, Quality of Evidence III — the category for expert opinion and descriptive studies — the search was English-language Medline only and closed in 2008, consensus was reached by email with no voting or agreement threshold, and the watch-and-wait strategy for inactive cysts is described by the authors themselves as deserving formal evaluation. Serology supports but does not establish the diagnosis, and a negative test does not exclude it. Note also that the AASLD liver biopsy paper states that careful aspiration of these lesions with a 19-gauge needle can be undertaken, with none of the precautions this consensus requires; where the two conflict, follow the echinococcosis consensus.

avoid.t: Do not put a needle into a cystic liver lesion that has a septum, a mural nodule or an enhancing wall.
avoid.pref: Image it properly, discuss it, and resect it if it is a mucinous cystic neoplasm.
avoid.avoid: Aspiration neither excludes the diagnosis nor treats it, and incomplete removal is the recognised cause of recurrence and malignant transformation in the reported series.

avoid.t: Do not give a simple cyst a surveillance interval.
avoid.pref: Call it benign, state the criteria it meets, and stop.
avoid.avoid: An interval attached to a definitively benign finding generates scans indefinitely and is the precise failure the ACR incidental-findings programme exists to prevent — the white paper's first two core recommendations are to forgo workup of lesions under 1 cm in low-risk patients and to forgo workup of lesions with distinctly benign features regardless of risk.

gates.name: 3 · Which test next, and what each one actually adds
crit: The lesion is solid and not resolved by the study in front of you
The available study lacked arterial-phase or delayed-phase imaging, or lacked contrast altogether
The question is a hepatocellular one — adenoma versus focal nodular hyperplasia, or HCC in an at-risk liver
The question is whether there is a second lesion anywhere else — a staging question, not a characterising one
The patient cannot have the obvious test: renal function, claustrophobia, pacemaker, pregnancy, body habitus
gates.ask: What exactly am I asking this scan, and is there a scan that answers it rather than one that repeats the last one?

standard.t: A multiphase contrast study is the characterising test, and the phases and the agent depend on the question — say which question you are asking when you order it.
standard.pref: Every solid lesion the index study left unresolved. The technical minimum, stated by the ACR Appropriateness Criteria and applying equally to CT, MRI and contrast-enhanced ultrasound, is at least two dynamic phases — late arterial and portal venous. The ACR white paper prefers MRI over CT for characterisation on three grounds: better assessment of internal features, more reliable assessment of enhancement, and no ionising radiation. EASL 2025 prefers CT or MRI over contrast-enhanced ultrasound as the first-line non-invasive test in at-risk patients because of higher sensitivity (LoE 3, strong recommendation).
standard.avoid: Do not read 'MRI is preferred' as a measured advantage. The ACR Appropriateness Criteria rate contrast-enhanced ultrasound, multiphase CT and contrast-enhanced MRI as equivalent and usually appropriate alternatives for an indeterminate lesion larger than 1 cm, both in a normal liver and in known chronic liver disease, and they do so on narrative accuracy ranges from different studies in different populations with no head-to-head data and no equivalence testing. The same document's own text cites specificity for contrast-enhanced CT in ultrasound-detected lesions as 38-82%, and one cited MRI study at 43% specificity for an exact diagnosis. A pathway that reads only the rating table never sees the 38%. And do not order 'MRI liver' and leave the agent to chance — the two guidelines ask for different agents for different questions, and that choice cannot be made by the scheduler.
standard.note: Where contrast is contraindicated, say what the unenhanced study can and cannot do rather than treating it as the characterising test. Note that the ACR Appropriateness Criteria and the ACR white paper, from the same organisation, use incompatible risk taxonomies: the white paper merges low and average risk into one low-risk tier, while the Appropriateness Criteria split high risk into chronic liver disease versus known extrahepatic malignancy. A pathway using both has to reconcile them, and this page does so by treating the liver-disease fork at gate 0 as primary.

standard.t: Contrast-enhanced ultrasound characterises a solid lesion in real time and is the right test when the question is vascular pattern rather than anatomy.
standard.pref: The lesion that is unclear after greyscale and Doppler ultrasound, the patient who cannot have gadolinium or iodinated contrast, and the small focal nodular hyperplasia where EASL puts CEUS ahead of MRI. The WFUMB guideline's single level-1 strong recommendation is for exactly this situation — contrast-enhanced ultrasound as the first-line technique for an incidentally detected indeterminate focal liver lesion at ultrasound in a non-cirrhotic liver without history or clinical suspicion of malignancy. In the DEGUM multicentre study of 1,349 patients at 14 hospitals with a hepatic lesion lacking a definite diagnosis on B-mode and power Doppler, overall accuracy against a reference standard that was histology in more than 75% of cases was 90.3%: 723 of 755 malignant lesions correctly assessed (sensitivity 95.8%) and 476 of 573 benign lesions (specificity 83.1%), with positive predictive value 95.4% and negative predictive value 95.7%.
standard.avoid: Carry both halves of that result and the limits of the recommendation behind it. Specificity was 83.1% — CEUS over-calls benign lesions as suspicious far more often than it misses cancer. In the companion analysis, 92 of the 1,349 lesions (6.8%) could not be definitively diagnosed by CEUS at all, mostly benign ones; the CEUS diagnosis was wrong in 39 lesions; and 8 lesions called benign by CEUS proved malignant — three histologically proven HCCs called adenoma, two called focal nodular hyperplasia that were an HCC and a metastasis, two called haemangioma that were an HCC and a metastasis, and one called benign that was a lymphoma. The WFUMB level-1 grade is asserted rather than demonstrated: no randomised comparison of CEUS-first against MRI-first for this lesion is cited, the supporting text is a block citation of roughly twenty studies with no pooled estimate or quality appraisal, and the guideline grades the same lesion in a patient with suspected malignancy as level 2 and only a weak recommendation — the higher-stakes scenario getting the weaker grade with no explanation.
standard.note: WFUMB in cooperation with EFSUMB, AFSUMB, AIUM and FLAUS updated the liver CEUS recommendations in 2020; that document, not the DEGUM study, is the protocol source, and it is the source to read on dose, mechanical index and the artefacts that cause mischaracterisation. Operator dependence is the unquantified variable: the guideline addresses it only through a training recommendation at its lowest evidence level, reports no interobserver agreement anywhere, and more than twenty of its authors declare relationships with the contrast or scanner manufacturers whose products the recommendations require. The DEGUM accuracy came from 14 centres using a standardised protocol, and CEUS LI-RADS category agreement is the lowest of any modality at kappa 0.30-0.39.

standard.t: In an at-risk liver, read the CEUS against CEUS LI-RADS v2017 criteria, not against the CT/MRI criteria — the washout timing and intensity are different and that is the whole point of the separate algorithm.
standard.pref: The cirrhotic or chronic hepatitis B patient whose nodule is being worked up by ultrasound. EASL 2025 gives the CEUS criterion explicitly — non-rim arterial hyperenhancement with late-onset washout (later than 60 seconds) of mild intensity (LoE 1). In a meta-analysis of 10 studies, 5,543 patients and 6,124 lesions including 4,492 HCCs, 97% (95-98) of CEUS LR-5 observations were HCC, and CEUS LR-5 had sensitivity 0.76 (0.70-0.81), specificity 0.95 (0.91-0.97) and accuracy 0.82 (0.75-0.88) for HCC.
standard.avoid: The categories are not interchangeable between modalities, and the evidence that they are not is weaker than the page previously implied. In a 43-study comparison, CEUS LR-3 was 21% HCC against 35% for CT/MRI LR-3 (p=0.02) and CEUS LR-M was 56% HCC against 33% (p=0.01), with non-HCC malignancy in LR-M 35% against 58% (p=0.01) — but few paired studies exist, so these are comparisons between different populations with different HCC prevalence and different reference standards, presented with p-values as though they were head-to-head tests. Heterogeneity across the pooled proportions is I-squared 78-93%, the authors concede meta-regression could not explain it, and the LR-3 proportion itself moves from 14% in Asian to 32% in non-Asian studies, which shows these are population artefacts rather than properties of the categories. The two meta-analyses this page used to make the point come from the same Tianjin department, share authors, grants and included studies, were published two months apart, and report CEUS LR-M as 44% and 56% HCC from largely the same primary literature — they are one body of work, not independent corroboration.
standard.note: CEUS LI-RADS remains at v2017 while CT/MRI LI-RADS is at v2018, and the diagnostic versions are not synchronised. For a CT or MRI observation that is LR-3 or non-characterizable, the prospective evidence that CEUS resolves it comes from one multicentre sub-analysis of 75 observations in 68 patients who were 97.1% cirrhotic — see gate 6, where the figures and their limits are set out. That study licenses nothing about a lesion in a liver that is not at risk.

opts.name: MRI with an extracellular gadolinium agent
opts.when: EASL 2025: extracellular contrast agents should be favoured over gadoxetic acid for the non-invasive diagnosis of HCC using MRI (LoE 1, strong recommendation, consensus). The ACR white paper likewise prefers gadolinium blood-pool agents generally.
opts.pref: The at-risk liver, where the diagnosis turns on true washout in the portal venous or delayed phase, and the haemangioma or focal nodular hyperplasia where delayed-phase fill-in and a delayed-enhancing central scar are the diagnostic features.
opts.avoid: It will not answer the adenoma-versus-focal-nodular-hyperplasia question, which needs hepatocyte uptake.
opts.note: The individual-patient-data meta-analysis that would have settled the agent question could not: only one contributing study made a direct within-observation comparison of extracellular against hepatobiliary agents, and the pooled dataset was skewed toward extracellular agents, so no comparative estimate exists.

opts.name: MRI with gadoxetate disodium (hepatobiliary agent)
opts.when: The ACR white paper recommends gadoxetate disodium specifically to distinguish focal nodular hyperplasia from hepatocellular adenoma, because focal nodular hyperplasia takes up the agent on the hepatobiliary phase and adenoma was thought not to. The white paper flags the question as important especially above 3 cm and subcapsular — a threshold its own 2010 predecessor set at 4 cm, with no new evidence cited for the change.
opts.pref: A solid hepatocellular lesion in a young woman in a normal liver, where the fork is focal nodular hyperplasia (discharge) versus adenoma (the HCA pathway).
opts.avoid: Two separate problems, and the first needs stating precisely because this page previously stated it loosely. In a meta-analysis of 28 studies, 364 patients and 410 subtyped adenomas, hepatobiliary-phase iso- or hyperintensity was present in 14% of all adenomas (95% CI 4-26%), in 0% of HNF1A-inactivated adenomas (0-2%), 14% of inflammatory (2-31%), 11% of unclassified (0-29%) and 59% of beta-catenin-activated adenomas (26-88%). Sensitivity and specificity for separating focal nodular hyperplasia from all adenoma subtypes together were 99% (57-100%) and 89% (82-94%); the much-quoted 65% specificity (44-80%) applies only once HNF1A-inactivated and inflammatory adenomas have already been excluded, so it is the specificity against an enriched residual population and not a measured property of the test in an unselected lesion. Second, in an at-risk liver EASL 2025 states that hypointensity on the transitional or hepatobiliary phase is an ancillary finding favouring malignancy in general, not the equivalent of washout, and that the agent carries a risk of respiratory motion artefact in the arterial phase — the phase the HCC diagnosis depends on.
opts.note: The B-HCA estimate rests on 33 lesions, 16 of the 28 included studies are case reports or small series, and no sensitivity analysis excluding them was performed — a case report of a beta-catenin adenoma gets written because it was hepatobiliary-phase hyperintense and surprised someone. The pairwise comparison that would matter most clinically, beta-catenin against inflammatory adenoma, did not separate them. The direction is clear and the precision is poor.

alt.order: Ordered by how often each is the right agent in an incidental population, not by any trial that compared them for this purpose. The order reflects guideline wording: EASL 2025 prefers the extracellular agent for the HCC question, and the ACR white paper prefers the hepatobiliary agent for the adenoma question. Both cannot be satisfied in one acquisition, which is why the question must be named on the request.
alt.flagnote: Ratification item: the programme needs a written rule for which agent is used when the question has not been narrowed — the at-risk liver, where EASL prefers an extracellular agent, versus the normal liver with a hepatocellular lesion, where the ACR prefers gadoxetate. The group should decide whether a hepatobiliary-phase iso-intense lesion may still be called focal nodular hyperplasia without tissue, and should do so on the right number: specificity against all adenoma subtypes is 89% (82-94%), falling to 65% (44-80%) only against beta-catenin-activated and unclassified adenoma once the other subtypes are excluded by conventional MRI. Audit: agent used, question stated on the request, and whether the study answered it.

alt.t: Where the index study is adequate and the lesion has distinctly benign features, order nothing.
alt.pref: The ACR benign-feature list on non-contrast or portal-venous-phase CT is a sharp margin with homogeneous low attenuation at or below 20 HU, or the characteristic appearance of haemangioma, focal nodular hyperplasia, focal fatty sparing or deposition, or a perfusion change. Any of those needs no follow-up regardless of risk category, and the first two of the white paper's four core recommendations say exactly that.
alt.avoid: Do not apply the list to a lesion with ill-defined margins, heterogeneous density, mural thickening or nodularity, thick septa, or intermediate-to-high attenuation above 20 HU on portal venous phase with pseudoenhancement excluded. Those features earn prompt MRI, not reassurance. And do not mistake the lists for measurements: sharp versus ill-defined margin, homogeneous versus heterogeneous density, thick versus thin septa and the judgement of whether pseudoenhancement is present are all reader calls on which the whole algorithm pivots, and no interobserver agreement is reported for any of them anywhere in either white paper. The 2010 document's own benign-feature footnote permits 'sharp but irregular margins' while its suspicious-feature footnote lists 'ill-defined margins', leaving irregular-but-sharp to the reader.
alt.note: Grade D, downgraded from C after the full-text read. This is a consensus feature list with no derivation and no reproducibility data, in a document whose committee states that its process meets no specific formal national standard and that its content should not be considered standard of care.

avoid.t: Do not use FDG PET to characterise a liver lesion.
avoid.pref: Use it to answer a distribution question in a patient with a known extrahepatic primary and a lesion larger than 1 cm found on non-contrast or single-phase imaging, which is the one scenario of eight that the ACR Appropriateness Criteria rate usually appropriate.
avoid.avoid: Per-lesion sensitivity for colorectal liver metastases was 81.4% (95% CI 66.5-90.6), statistically indistinguishable from MRI at 80.3%, and the FDG PET/CT data specifically came down to one per-lesion data set. The white paper's own claim is modest — PET may preclude biopsy in some patients with lesions larger than 1 cm — and the Appropriateness Criteria rate PET usually not appropriate in a normal liver on the stated ground that no relevant literature supports it there.

avoid.t: Do not repeat the same inadequate study with the same protocol.
avoid.pref: Name the deficiency — missing arterial phase, missing delayed phase, aggressive dose reduction, no contrast — and order the study that fixes it.
avoid.avoid: A second single-phase CT answers nothing and is the commonest wasted step in this pathway. The local master workup CPG requires the multidisciplinary team to document whether repeat imaging is needed when image quality or protocol is inadequate, rather than proceeding on a study that cannot support the decision.

gates.name: 4 · Haemangioma and focal nodular hyperplasia — resolved and discharged here
crit: Haemangioma on ultrasound: homogeneously hyperechoic, sharp margin, posterior acoustic enhancement, no halo sign, under 3 cm, in a normal liver

Haemangioma on contrast imaging: peripheral globular arterial enhancement with progressive central fill-in on delayed phases; strongly hyperintense on heavily T2-weighted MRI with a high apparent diffusion coefficient

Focal nodular hyperplasia: homogeneous except for a central scar, near-isodense before contrast, strong homogeneous arterial enhancement becoming isodense on portal venous and delayed phases, no capsule, lobulated contour
Central scar hyperintense on T2 and enhancing on delayed phase with an extracellular agent
No underlying vascular liver disease, and no feature on the suspicious list
gates.ask: Can I name this lesion and send the patient away today, without an interval?

standard.t: In a normal liver, a hyperechoic lesion under 3 cm with a sharp margin, posterior acoustic enhancement and no halo sign is a haemangioma on ultrasound alone, and no contrast study is needed.
standard.pref: The asymptomatic patient with no liver disease and no cancer. This is EASL's recommendation at evidence level II-2, grade of recommendation 1, and the prior probability is consistent with it — haemangioma was the third commonest of five pre-specified benign findings in 45,319 university-hospital ultrasound examinations, 1,640 cases, mean size 20.1 mm, after focal fatty sparing (2,839, 6.26%) and cysts (2,631, 5.81%).
standard.avoid: EASL draws the line itself: in oncology patients or in those with underlying liver disease, contrast-enhanced imaging is required (II-2, grade 1). The ultrasound-only rule does not cross into either of those populations. And do not treat the prevalence as a fixed quantity — EASL's own figure for haemangioma is a range of 0.4% to 20% of the general population, around 5% in imaging series and up to 20% at autopsy, and the 45,319-patient series reports its haemangioma rate as 3.3% in the abstract and 3.62% in the results table and Table 3, of which only the latter matches 1,640 of 45,319.
standard.note: Discharge rule: because of its benign course, imaging follow-up is not required for a typical haemangioma (II-2, grade 1), and pregnancy and oral contraceptives are not contraindicated (III, grade 2). Conservative management is appropriate for typical cases (II-2, grade 1). Worth knowing when quoting the grades: not one recommendation anywhere in that guideline rests on evidence level I or II-1, so there is no randomised or controlled evidence behind any of it, and there is no stated search strategy, database or date range underneath the GRADE labels.

standard.t: Where ultrasound is atypical, diagnose the haemangioma on MRI — peripheral and globular arterial enhancement with central fill-in on delayed phases, strong T2 hyperintensity, high apparent diffusion coefficient — and then discharge it.
standard.pref: Rapidly filling and giant haemangiomas, the two commonest atypias, are both readily diagnosed on MRI. EASL reports MRI sensitivity and specificity for haemangioma above 90%.
standard.avoid: Know the named pitfalls. High-flow haemangiomas imaged with gadoxetic acid can show relatively low signal against liver on the three-minute equilibrium phase — a pseudo-washout that mimics a hypervascular tumour; the discriminators are very strong T2 signal and arterial-phase enhancement. Cystic, pedunculated, fluid-fluid-level, calcified, hyalinised or very slowly filling haemangiomas are the rare group in which imaging including MRI is explicitly less reliable, and small haemangiomas may show uniform flash filling that the ACR algorithm treats differently by risk category.
standard.note: Size does not create follow-up. EASL states there is no relationship between haemangioma size and complications, and little relationship between symptoms and lesion characteristics; no randomised trial shows resection better than conservative management. Kasabach-Merritt syndrome, a growing lesion, or symptoms from compression are the referral triggers (III, grade 1).

standard.t: Focal nodular hyperplasia can be diagnosed with nearly 100% specificity when the typical features are seen in combination, and a typical lesion needs no follow-up at all unless there is underlying vascular liver disease.
standard.pref: The young woman with a lobulated, homogeneous, arterially enhancing lesion with a T2-bright central scar that enhances late. EASL: CEUS, CT or MRI can diagnose focal nodular hyperplasia with nearly 100% specificity when typical features are seen in combination (II-2, grade 1); MRI has the highest overall performance, and CEUS the highest accuracy below 3 cm (II-2, grade 1). It is also an uncommon incidental finding — 81 cases (0.18%) in 45,319 hospital ultrasound examinations, against 19 (0.04%) for adenoma — so an incidental hepatocellular lesion is far more often focal nodular hyperplasia than adenoma, but neither is a random discovery.
standard.avoid: The sensitivity is the weak half: MRI sensitivity is 70-80% and lower in small lesions where the central scar is usually absent, so a lesion without the full feature set is neither excluded as focal nodular hyperplasia nor diagnosed as it. EASL's rule is that in atypical cases, liver biopsy is indicated. Steatotic focal nodular hyperplasia mimics adenoma and is commoner in a steatotic liver; strong T2 hyperintensity, a pseudocapsule and washout are the other recognised atypias. Be careful with the two prevalence figures as well: in that series both focal nodular hyperplasia and adenoma required confirmation by CEUS, MRI or histology while cysts, haemangiomas and fatty sparing were accepted on B-mode alone, and the mean confirmed lesion sizes were 51.6 mm and 39.0 mm — far larger than a typical incidental lesion. Asymmetric ascertainment of the rare entities is the likeliest reason both figures came in roughly tenfold below every prior series, including EASL's own 0.4-3% at autopsy and 0.03% clinically relevant for focal nodular hyperplasia.
standard.note: Discharge rule: where the diagnosis is firm and the patient asymptomatic, follow-up imaging is not required and the patient can be discharged (III, grade 2). There is no indication to discontinue oral contraceptives and no need for follow-up during pregnancy. Treatment is not recommended (II-3, grade 2). The 'nearly 100% specificity' claim carries no pooled estimate and no confidence interval in the guideline.

alt.t: Where the hepatocellular lesion cannot be separated from adenoma on an extracellular-agent study, add a hepatobiliary-phase study — but grade the result by what it can and cannot exclude.
alt.pref: The indeterminate hepatocellular lesion where the fork is discharge versus the HCA pathway. EASL reports that hepatobiliary agents raise sensitivity for focal nodular hyperplasia to about 90%, with sensitivity and specificity for separating it from adenoma of 92–96.9% and 91–100% in the primary studies.
alt.avoid: EASL itself flags that the supporting meta-analysis rested on few, heterogeneous studies at high risk of bias, and the subsequent subtype-stratified meta-analysis shows where the specificity goes. Hepatobiliary-phase iso- or hyperintensity occurs in 0% of HNF1A-inactivated adenomas (95% CI 0-2%), 14% of inflammatory (2-31%) and 59% of beta-catenin-activated adenomas (26-88%). Specificity for focal nodular hyperplasia against all adenoma subtypes together is 89% (82-94%); it falls to 65% (44-80%) only against beta-catenin-activated and unclassified adenoma, after conventional MRI has already excluded the two commoner subtypes. State it that way round. Either way, a hepatobiliary-phase iso-intense lesion does not exclude the adenoma subtype with the highest malignant potential, and the paired sensitivity figures of 99% carry intervals of 57-100% and 53-100%, which are not measurements.
alt.note: The authors' own explanation is that the low prevalence of beta-catenin-activated adenoma produced the earlier high performance figures. Thirty-three beta-catenin-activated adenomas across 28 studies, 16 of which were case reports or small series, is a thin basis for a 59% estimate, and all four studies supplying the diagnostic-performance figures were case-control in design and marked high risk of bias for patient selection — so the specificity numbers are functions of the sampling as much as of the test. It is the direction, not the precision, that matters for the discharge decision.

alt.t: Where focal nodular hyperplasia is multiple, look for the setting rather than counting the lesions.
alt.pref: Focal nodular hyperplasia is multiple in 20-30% of cases and associated with liver haemangioma in 20%. Multiple lesions should prompt a search for an underlying vascular liver disease — Budd-Chiari syndrome, obliterative portal venopathy or porto-sinusoidal vascular disorder, hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia, portal vein agenesis — in which EASL's own discharge rule no longer applies. The reason is quantitative: imaging displays hepatic nodules in 60-80% of patients with Budd-Chiari syndrome, usually under 4 cm, frequently more than ten, hypervascular and disseminated throughout a non-cirrhotic liver.
alt.avoid: Do not treat multiplicity as evidence of malignancy, and do not discharge multiple focal nodular hyperplasia without asking why there are several. But do not read the 60-80% as a post-test probability either: it is the prevalence of nodules among patients already known to have Budd-Chiari syndrome, and neither guideline reports the inverse — the probability of underlying vascular disease given multiple hypervascular nodules in a non-cirrhotic liver. That conditional, which is the one a radiologist needs, does not exist in either document.
alt.note: EASL's wording is precise: for a lesion typical of focal nodular hyperplasia follow-up is not necessary, unless there is underlying vascular liver disease (III, grade 2). It does not say what the interval should be in that case, and neither does this page. Grade D, downgraded from C: the rule is a III / grade 2 recommendation on one side and a superseded 2015 vascular-disease guideline on the other.

avoid.t: Do not biopsy a typical haemangioma, and do not biopsy a typical focal nodular hyperplasia.
avoid.pref: Diagnose on imaging, name the features, discharge. Where the diagnosis genuinely cannot be reached on imaging, EASL accepts percutaneous biopsy of a haemangioma provided a cuff of normal parenchyma lies between the capsule and the lesion margin, reporting an overall diagnostic accuracy of 96%.
avoid.avoid: The procedure is not free, it does not alter management in a typical lesion, and both EASL recommendations state that these are invasive procedures with risk that should only be pursued after consideration by an experienced multidisciplinary team.

avoid.t: Do not attach a surveillance interval to a typical haemangioma or focal nodular hyperplasia because the lesion is large.
avoid.pref: Discharge, with a plain explanation that the lesion may change size and that a slow incidental increase is not a cause for concern where the diagnosis is solid.
avoid.avoid: EASL states that haemangiomas may change size during long-term follow-up with no relationship between size and complications, and that focal nodular hyperplasia is stable over time in the vast majority of cases. Size-triggered surveillance of these two lesions generates scans without generating decisions.

gates.name: 5 · Pseudolesions and nodules of the diseased liver — nothing to follow
crit: Focal fat or focal fat sparing in a characteristic site — adjacent to the falciform ligament or ligamentum venosum, the gallbladder fossa, the porta hepatis, or subcapsular
Geometric or straight-edged margin, no displacement of traversing vessels, no mass effect
A transient hepatic attenuation or intensity difference — peripheral, wedge-shaped, present on one phase only
A regenerative nodule in a cirrhotic liver with no major feature and nothing suspicious
A regenerative or focal-nodular-hyperplasia-like nodule in a liver with a vascular disorder
gates.ask: Is this actually a lesion, or is it normal liver behaving differently from the liver next to it?

standard.t: Focal fat and focal fat sparing in a characteristic location with no vessel displacement and no mass effect are definitively characterised on the study in front of you and need no follow-up.
standard.pref: The commonest finding of all — focal fatty sparing was the single largest contributor to the 15.1% benign-finding rate in 45,319 university-hospital ultrasound examinations, 2,839 cases (6.26%), mean size 20.6 mm, every one of them solitary and every one of them in the segment IV and gallbladder-bed location. It is a pseudolesion rather than a tumour, which is part of why that 15.1% figure cannot be read as a lesion prevalence. The ACR white paper states that the characteristic locations enable definitive characterisation without further follow-up, naming the region near the falciform ligament and the gallbladder fossa. The pattern review adds the diagnostic features: the distribution is heterogeneous or non-uniform, the margin may be geometric, and traversing vessels are not displaced.
standard.avoid: Know the patterns that do not look like this. Multinodular and perivascular fat accumulation are specifically described as mimicking neoplastic, inflammatory or vascular conditions, and patchy foci of normal parenchyma in an otherwise fatty liver can be a genuinely difficult problem. Where the pattern is nodular rather than geometric, treat it as unresolved and go to gate 3.
standard.note: Chemical-shift or fat-fraction MRI settles the question directly when it matters; opposed-phase signal loss confirms fat.

standard.t: A transient hepatic attenuation or intensity difference is a perfusion phenomenon, not a mass: recognise it by its peripheral location, wedge shape and single-phase behaviour, and report no follow-up.
standard.pref: The peripheral wedge of altered enhancement on the arterial phase that is invisible on the portal venous phase. The white paper's position is that characteristic locations and enhancement features allow definitive recognition and that these require no follow-up.
standard.avoid: A true lesion can sit at the apex of a perfusion abnormality, particularly in an at-risk liver, and a uniformly flash-filling observation is treated differently by risk category — in a high-risk patient the white paper advises MRI routinely for flash-filling lesions because of a higher probability of malignancy, while noting that in cirrhosis the majority of small wedge-shaped hypervascular lesions remain benign.
standard.note: The phrase to avoid in a report is 'cannot exclude a lesion' when the finding is confined to one phase and has no counterpart on any other sequence.

standard.t: A nodule in a cirrhotic liver with no arterial hyperenhancement and no other major feature is a regenerative or dysplastic nodule in all probability, and LI-RADS already states what to do with it — do not improvise an interval.
standard.pref: The 8 mm or 15 mm nodule found on a surveillance or incidental study in a cirrhotic liver. Under CT/MRI LI-RADS v2018 the no-arterial-hyperenhancement observations fall into LR-2 or LR-3 depending on size and feature count, and the management LI-RADS specifies is repeat or alternative diagnostic imaging in 3 to 6 months for LR-3, not discharge and not biopsy.
standard.avoid: Do not describe either category as benign to the patient, and do not treat the numbers as precise. In the pooled systematic review, 13% (95% CI 8-22) of LR-2 and 38% (31-45) of LR-3 observations were confirmed HCC, and 14% (9-21) and 40% (31-50) respectively were confirmed malignant — a 3-to-6-month interval on a 38% probability is a watch, not reassurance. The authors explicitly label the LR-2 estimate provisional and at high risk of bias, and it rests on 223 observations for HCC and 162 for malignancy.
standard.note: Two cautions on how the category is reached. The feature that most often lifts a nodule out of LR-2 or LR-3 on a follow-up study is threshold growth, and the 2022 individual-patient-data meta-analysis found no association between threshold growth and HCC (OR 1.6, 95% CI 0.8-3.4) — assessable in only 452 of 4,434 observations, and reported a second time in the same paper as 1.6 (0.7-3.6). Enhancing capsule is weak too, OR 2.4 (1.7-3.5), and reached significance in only one of the three analysis cohorts. Downgraded from B to C: every figure here comes from retrospective cohorts with structural verification bias. A cirrhotic liver with a nodule is, by definition, a liver that needs surveillance anyway; the surveillance programme and the nodule's follow-up interval should be one plan with one owner, not two.

alt.t: In a liver with a vascular disorder, treat regenerative and focal-nodular-hyperplasia-like nodules as a specific entity to be managed under the vascular-liver-disease guideline, with an interval set by the multidisciplinary team rather than copied from LI-RADS.
alt.pref: Budd-Chiari syndrome, obliterative portal venopathy, congenital portosystemic shunt, cardiac congestion, and what is now called porto-sinusoidal vascular disorder or non-cirrhotic portal fibrosis. These livers generate multiple arterially hyperenhancing benign nodules, LI-RADS explicitly excludes them from its population, and EASL's benign-tumour guideline removes its own no-follow-up rule for focal nodular hyperplasia in this setting.
alt.avoid: Neither guideline states an interval for this situation. Setting one is a local decision and should be recorded as such rather than presented as guideline-derived. One thing has changed since this page was drafted and it changes what a report can safely say: the 2026 multisociety consensus makes nodular regenerative hyperplasia one of three major histological criteria for porto-sinusoidal vascular disorder, alongside muscularised portal venules and portal venule stenosis in 50% or more of portal tracts. Nodular regenerative hyperplasia is therefore no longer a benign nodular tumour to reassure a patient about; it is a marker of a vascular disorder, and EASL's benign-tumour guideline had already placed it outside its own scope on exactly that ground.
alt.note: Grade D, and labelled as an operating rule rather than a result. Take the 2026 consensus for what it is: liver biopsy is mandatory for the diagnosis (95% agreement) with adequacy set at a 15 mm specimen including one fragment of 10 mm or more, but the criteria were derived in 88 European patients who all had specific signs of portal hypertension while the definition permits diagnosis without portal hypertension — which is exactly the patient an incidental nodular liver produces — a major criterion needs a sensitivity of only 0.10 provided specificity exceeds 0.95, and the diagnostic score was fitted to votes on 36 hypothetical scenarios and then shown to reproduce those votes, which is arithmetic consistency rather than diagnostic validity. The consensus says nothing about how incidentally detected nodular regenerative hyperplasia should be handled, and nothing about the harms of biopsying incidental nodularity. The EASL vascular-liver guidance this page otherwise relies on is the 2015 edition, superseded by a 2026 edition not obtained for this page. See the honest section and the approvals list.

alt.t: Where a pseudolesion cannot be distinguished from a mass on the available study, re-image on the modality that answers the mechanism rather than repeating the one that raised the question.
alt.pref: Chemical-shift MRI for a suspected fat phenomenon; a properly phased multiphase study for a suspected perfusion phenomenon. Both answer a mechanism question that a second unenhanced CT cannot.
alt.avoid: Do not put a pseudolesion into a surveillance programme because the index study was ambiguous. Resolve it once.

avoid.t: Do not biopsy a geometric area of altered attenuation in a fatty liver.
avoid.pref: Confirm with chemical-shift imaging and report it as a fat phenomenon.
avoid.avoid: The histology comes back as liver, the patient has had a procedure for nothing, and the next clinician reads the result as an inadequate sample.

avoid.t: Do not call a sub-centimetre nodule in a cirrhotic liver benign.
avoid.pref: Assign the LI-RADS category, state the category's own management interval, and make sure the surveillance programme owns it.
avoid.avoid: LR-1 is the only category in which no malignancy was found in the pooled review. LR-2 at 13% (95% CI 8-22) HCC and LR-3 at 38% (31-45) are not benign. The systematic review's authors do argue those figures indicate the need for a more active management strategy than the categories currently recommend — but they also call the LR-2 estimate provisional and at high risk of bias two paragraphs earlier, so this page states the number and does not adopt the recommendation.

gates.name: 6 · The lesion imaging cannot characterise
crit: Under 10 mm, and reported as too small to characterise
Seen on one modality and not on another, with no explanation for the discrepancy
Indeterminate after an adequate multiphase MRI
LR-3 or LR-4 in an at-risk liver, where the category is itself a statement of uncertainty
Indeterminate in a patient whose treatment decision cannot wait for an interval
gates.ask: Does this lesion need to be resolved now, and if an interval is the answer, what exactly will I do differently when it comes back unchanged?

standard.t: Decide before you set an interval what a stable repeat scan will change, and write that down.
standard.pref: Every indeterminate lesion. If the answer is that stability discharges the patient, say so and name the interval. If the answer is that stability changes nothing because the lesion will be resected either way, go to gate 7 or gate 8 now.
standard.avoid: An interval set without a stopping rule becomes indefinite surveillance. The ACR Incidental Findings Committee exists because of exactly this cascade — its founding paper describes the inclination to evaluate incidental findings as driven by physician and patient unwillingness to accept uncertainty, and names the potentially injurious and expensive cascade of tests and procedures as the harm.
standard.note: Grade D by construction. No trial compares interval strategies for the indeterminate liver lesion, and this is an operating rule the programme chooses.

standard.t: A new sub-centimetre lesion in a patient with cancer, cirrhosis or other hepatic risk factors gets MRI at 3 to 6 months; the same lesion in a patient with no risk factor gets nothing.
standard.pref: This is the ACR algorithm's most consequential single rule and it follows the risk fork at gate 0, not the lesion. In a low-risk patient, lesions 1 cm or smaller require no workup at all. In a high-risk patient, MRI is advised in 3 to 6 months to characterise the lesion and assess growth, and for a sub-centimetre lesion found on ultrasound in a patient with a known extrahepatic malignancy the ACR Appropriateness Criteria make MRI without and with contrast the only option they rate usually appropriate.
standard.avoid: Four honest qualifications, and the first is the most important. Every number in this rule is a convention. The small-lesion stratum was 0.5 cm in the 2010 white paper and 1 cm in 2017; the interval was 6 months and became 3 to 6 months; the three risk tiers became two; the focal-nodular-hyperplasia-versus-adenoma threshold moved from 4 cm to 3 cm. Four thresholds changed in seven years with no new evidence cited and the same subcommittee chair on both occasions, and the committee states that its consensus process meets no specific formal national standard and that its content should not be considered standard of care. Second, the test being ordered is not reliable at that size: per-lesion sensitivity for colorectal metastases below 10 mm was 60.2% for MRI and 47.3% for CT. Third, in the 2,978-patient cancer cohort, 8.2% of small lesions were followed for under 6 months, remained stable and were still classed indeterminate — so a 3-month repeat often resolves nothing. Fourth, the white paper permits the radiologist to deviate from the under-1-cm rule even in low-risk patients when a lesion has suspicious features, in which case MRI is suggested.
standard.note: Growth over a year is concerning; growth over a shorter timeframe is more urgent. That is the white paper's wording and it is a judgement, not a threshold — and growth was deliberately left out of the algorithm altogether because thresholds vary by risk category, then reinserted as narrative advice. Downgraded from C to D: an underived consensus threshold is grade D however firmly it is stated.

standard.t: A lesion that exists on one modality and not on another is a finding about the two studies, not about the liver — reconcile the studies before you work up the lesion.
standard.pref: Compare the actual images side by side with the radiologist, not the two reports. Check phase timing, slice thickness, dose, breath-hold position, field of view and whether the segment was covered at all. Most one-modality lesions resolve as a timing or coverage difference, a perfusion phenomenon, or a lesion that one modality cannot show.
standard.avoid: There is no literature that quantifies how often a one-modality-only liver lesion proves malignant, and targeted searching does not find one — this page should not imply there is. What is documented is that even with a standardised protocol and a histological reference standard in a 1,349-patient multicentre study, 6.8% of lesions that were unclear on greyscale ultrasound could not be definitively diagnosed by contrast-enhanced ultrasound either, and most of those were benign. Residual uncertainty is normal and is not by itself a reason to escalate.
standard.note: The local master workup CPG requires baseline and restaging studies used for selection to be available for central review with the priors, and requires the team to document whether repeat imaging is needed when the protocol was inadequate. Reconciliation is a named step, not an informal courtesy.

alt.t: Where the lesion is LR-3 or LR-4 in an at-risk liver, use the category's own management pathway and put the case in front of the board rather than inventing a plan.
alt.pref: LI-RADS v2018 specifies repeat or alternative diagnostic imaging in 3 to 6 months for LR-3, and multidisciplinary discussion with consideration of biopsy or shorter-interval imaging for LR-4. The pooled malignancy figures justify the difference — 40% (95% CI 31-50) of LR-3 and 80% (75-85) of LR-4 observations were confirmed malignant. Where the unresolved observation is in a cirrhotic liver, contrast-enhanced ultrasound is a reasonable next step before an interval is set: in a prospective multicentre cohort of 75 CT/MRI-indeterminate observations in 68 patients, CEUS re-categorised 25 of 75 (33.3%) with a management change that was correct in 24 of 25 (96.0%), and avoided follow-up imaging altogether in 21 of 75 (28.0%).
alt.avoid: Do not treat LR-4 as a diagnosis and do not treat it as benign.
