It is 74% (67-80) HCC and 80% malignant in pooled retrospective data with acknowledged verification bias, which is exactly the range in which a board decision beats an algorithm. And do not over-read the CEUS study. Its population was 97.1% cirrhotic with 23.5% having a personal history of HCC, enrolled because a lesion had already been found — the baseline risk in that cohort was 25.9% HCC for a CT/MRI LR-3 observation and 52.4% for a non-characterizable one. In a liver that is not at risk the same appearances carry a far lower probability and none of those predictive values holds. The quoted 100% positive and negative predictive values rest on 7, 7, 6 and 1 observations with no confidence interval anywhere in the paper — 7 of 7 has an exact interval of roughly 59-100%. CEUS readers could see the CT or MRI in most cases, the reference standard was follow-up CT or MRI in 72% of observations, persistently LR-3 nodules at one year were counted non-malignant, and 74.1% of LR-3 observations remained indeterminate after CEUS. The study was funded in part by the manufacturer of the contrast agent.
alt.note: A lesion with both hepatocellular and cholangiocytic phenotypes, or an LR-M observation, goes to gate 8 and to the cHCC-CCA pathway, not into an interval. Downgraded from B to C: the LI-RADS management figures are retrospective and the CEUS evidence is a sub-analysis of a trial powered for a different question.

alt.t: Where an interval is chosen, name the owner, the date and the modality in the record, and close the loop in the registry.
alt.pref: Every deferred lesion. The failure this prevents is the common one: an interval recommended in a radiology report that no clinician owns.
alt.avoid: Do not leave the interval in the impression of a report as the only record of it. The local master workup CPG requires an assigned owner and due date for any conditional or incomplete disposition, and requires that such a case not be presented as approved.

avoid.t: Do not keep re-imaging a lesion when the answer will not change management.
avoid.pref: Either resolve it with tissue, or resect it, or discharge it, and say which.
avoid.avoid: Repeated imaging of a stable indeterminate lesion is the pathway's commonest way to spend a year. The ACR's founding incidental-findings paper puts standardisation forward precisely to limit cost and reduce risk to patients from this cascade.

avoid.t: Do not resolve diagnostic uncertainty by escalating to a more invasive test before the cheaper one has been done properly.
avoid.pref: An adequate multiphase MRI with the right agent, read against the right criteria, resolves most of these. Biopsy follows a failed adequate study, not a failed inadequate one.
avoid.avoid: The ACR algorithm reserves direct biopsy for large, highly suspicious lesions in high-risk patients and otherwise recommends prompt MRI at minimum.

gates.name: 7 · Biopsy — when it adds something, and when it costs an option
crit: The destination is named before any needle is passed: resection, transplant pathway, systemic therapy, or discharge
The result will change management — not merely confirm what the plan already assumes
The lesion is not a resectable colorectal metastasis, and the patient is not a candidate for a perihilar transplant protocol
Suspected perihilar cholangiocarcinoma has been excluded, or the transplant pathway has been reviewed first
Core biopsy rather than fine-needle aspiration, with the route and the specimen priorities agreed in advance
gates.ask: Will this result change what I do, and will the route I am about to use cost this patient an option they currently have?

standard.t: Do not perform a transperitoneal or primary-tumour needle biopsy in a patient with suspected perihilar cholangiocarcinoma until the transplant pathway has been reviewed — this is the local programme's written safety rule and it is not a weighing of evidence.
standard.pref: Any central, periductal or hilar lesion with biliary dilatation above it. The local Master Workup and Staging CPG carries this as its one critical safety rule, requires suspected perihilar disease to be flagged before any primary-tumour biopsy at the safety-screen step, requires regional-node sampling to follow the perihilar protocol, and requires the biopsy route to be documented for all cholangiocarcinoma candidates. From here the case is the perihilar cholangiocarcinoma pathway, which carries the route rules in full.
standard.avoid: The supporting data are retrospective, small, and asymmetrically evidenced. Of 191 patients in a neoadjuvant-plus-transplant protocol, 16 had a transperitoneal fine-needle aspiration of the primary elsewhere; of the 6 whose aspirate was positive for adenocarcinoma, 5 of 6 (83%) had peritoneal metastases at operative staging, against 8% (14 of 175) in those not biopsied, p=0.0097. The 9 patients with non-diagnostic aspirates had no metastases — which means the excess fell entirely on diagnostic aspirates and reverse causation is not excluded. Six patients is not a measured seeding rate. Note the asymmetry in the surgical literature too: the seeding risk that justifies the prohibition is asserted with no rate and no denominator anywhere, while the competing harm is quantified — about 15% of patients resected for apparent perihilar cholangiocarcinoma prove on final pathology to have benign disease, a figure the review states twice from a single citation with no denominator or interval of its own.
standard.note: The surgical review of this disease states the general position plainly: biopsy is typically avoided because of the risk of seeding metastases and the low yield of a bile duct brush, it is contraindicated outright in a transplant candidate, and a negative brushing or biopsy should not exclude the diagnosis or delay treatment. Read the review for what it is — a narrative paper by hepatobiliary and transplant surgeons with no search strategy, no quality appraisal and survival figures drawn entirely from uncontrolled surgical series — and take the safety rule from the local CPG rather than from it.

standard.t: Do not biopsy a lesion you are going to resect anyway.
standard.pref: The resectable colorectal liver metastasis in a patient with a confirmed colorectal primary, the resectable solitary mass in a fit patient where the operation is the same whatever the histology shows, and the lesion whose imaging phenotype and clinical context leave no competing diagnosis that would change the plan.
standard.avoid: The quantitative case rests on two different kinds of evidence and they are not equally strong. For colorectal metastases, 17 of 90 biopsied patients (19%) had needle-track deposits and 4-year survival was 32.5% against 46.7%, p=0.008 — in a retrospective comparison in which every biopsy was done at a referring hospital, synchronous disease was present in 61% of the biopsied against 26% of the non-biopsied (p<0.001) with no multivariable adjustment, and the denominator is conditioned on having reached a resection. For hepatocellular carcinoma, a meta-analysis of 8 observational studies put needle-track seeding at 2.7% per patient (95% CI 1.8-4.0) or 0.9% per patient per year (0.6-1.3), with no case demonstrably affecting survival — but seven of the eight studies were retrospective, the largest and only prospective one found zero events in 239 patients, median follow-up in several series was shorter than the 17-month median time to seeding, and the abstract misstates its own units by a factor of 100. Do not quote one number for both diseases.
standard.note: Procedural harm is quoted inconsistently across every source this page uses, and the group should know that before it writes a consent line. The ACR white paper gives morbidity of about 0.5% and mortality about 0.05% and prefers core biopsy over fine-needle aspiration; the same committee's 2010 document gave morbidity of 2.0% to 4.8%, with no explanation for the revision. The AASLD position paper gives severe bleeding at 1 in 2,500 to 1 in 10,000 and mortality at about 1 in 10,000 — but explicitly for the intercostal percutaneous approach in diffuse non-focal disease, while noting that death from bleeding may be greater after biopsy of a malignant lesion — and gives tumour seeding as 0.13% from one study, twenty-fold below the pooled HCC figure. If the route under discussion is endoscopic ultrasound-guided fine-needle biopsy, a meta-analysis of 99 studies and 9,303 patients puts the overall adverse-event rate at 1.8% but the liver subgroup at 14.0% (95% CI 7.7-24.0) — on 133 patients in 4 studies with 18 events, 13 of which were abdominal pain, 3 bleeds and one suspected death from anticoagulant interruption that the paper's own conclusion denies occurred. No source in this depot reports comparable harm figures for the competing routes, which is a ratification item rather than a finding.

standard.t: Biopsy is the right move when imaging criteria cannot be applied or have failed, and the result will change the plan — and in a liver that is not at risk, that is the guideline position rather than a fallback.
standard.pref: The indeterminate solid lesion in a non-cirrhotic liver; the lesion that remains indeterminate after an adequate multiphase MRI; the at-risk patient whose observation does not meet LR-5. EASL 2025 states that HCC diagnosis should be confirmed by tumour biopsy when the non-invasive imaging-based diagnostic criteria are not met (LoE 1), and that in patients without cirrhosis, chronic HBV or a history of HCC the diagnosis must be confirmed by biopsy. The ACR white paper's indication is the same shape — when MRI cannot confirm the diagnosis and the knowledge would alter management.
standard.avoid: Do not biopsy to document a diagnosis nobody will act on. And do not biopsy without agreeing the specimen priorities first — the local CPG requires tissue priorities to be defined before limited material is consumed, in the order diagnostic confirmation, required biomarkers, broad sequencing, research, and tumour-informed circulating-tumour-DNA assay creation.
standard.note: Route, platelet count, coagulation, ascites and the choice between percutaneous, transjugular and laparoscopic access are governed by the AASLD liver biopsy position paper and by local interventional radiology policy. EASL 2025 also asks that, if a biopsy is obtained, prognostic features including tumour differentiation and WHO subtype be reported (LoE 1, strong recommendation).

alt.t: Where the lesion is hepatocellular and the question is which adenoma subtype, accept that biopsy answers a question imaging increasingly cannot, and send the case to the HCA pathway with the subtype question stated.
alt.pref: A hepatobiliary-phase iso-intense hepatocellular lesion in a normal liver, where 59% (95% CI 26-88%) of beta-catenin-activated adenomas show that same appearance and the hepatobiliary phase cannot separate beta-catenin-activated from inflammatory adenoma at all. The subtype decides risk, and this is the HCA pathway from here.
alt.avoid: Do not biopsy a lesion that is already going to be resected on size or sex criteria — the explant or resection specimen answers the subtype question without a needle.
alt.note: The ACR white paper's own subtype summary — inflammatory adenoma carrying the greatest haemorrhage risk and beta-catenin-activated adenoma the greatest malignancy risk — is the reason the subtype matters. EASL goes further and states that beta-catenin-activated adenoma cannot be identified, or distinguished from unclassified adenoma or from HCC, by any imaging technique, while simultaneously making a proven beta-catenin mutation an indication for resection. That circularity is the reason the question reaches a needle at all, and the HCA pathway carries it.

alt.t: Where the result will not change management but the diagnosis is needed for a trial, a registry or a protocol, say that is the reason.
alt.pref: Protocol-mandated tissue, molecular profiling for a named systemic therapy decision, or the assay-creation requirement for tumour-informed circulating tumour DNA. Naming the reason makes the risk-benefit explicit and makes the consent accurate.
alt.avoid: Do not fold a protocol-driven biopsy into the clinical indication. They have different thresholds and different consent conversations.

avoid.t: Do not biopsy before the destination has been named.
avoid.pref: Resection, transplant pathway, systemic therapy or discharge — one of those, written down, before the needle.
avoid.avoid: A biopsy obtained for convenience is the commonest way a curative option is lost in this pathway, and the local CPG's safety screen exists to catch it.

avoid.t: Do not accept a non-diagnostic result as reassurance.
avoid.pref: Decide in advance what a negative or non-diagnostic result will change. If the answer is nothing, the patient needs a destination decision, not another needle.
avoid.avoid: In the perihilar series the 9 non-diagnostic aspirates had no metastases while 5 of 6 diagnostic ones did — the same procedure, two entirely different implications — and the yield of brush cytology and biopsy in biliary strictures is low enough that the surgical review states plainly a negative result should not exclude the diagnosis or delay treatment. The same holds for a small nodule: in the one prospective series inside the hepatocellular-carcinoma seeding meta-analysis, 294 nodules of 2 cm or less were biopsied, 49 (17%) yielded no diagnosis, and 29 of those (10% of the whole series) later proved to be HCC that the aspirate had missed — 8 inadequate samples, 11 read as regenerative and 10 as dysplastic.

gates.name: 8 · Routing — name the destination page
crit: LR-5, or LR-4 after board discussion, in an at-risk liver
An LR-M or targetoid observation, or a peripheral mass with capsular retraction and delayed central enhancement
A confirmed colorectal or neuroendocrine primary
A hepatocellular lesion in a normal liver that is not focal nodular hyperplasia
A lesion carrying both hepatocellular and cholangiocytic phenotypes, or discordant markers
gates.ask: Which page does this patient belong on, and have I named it rather than describing it?

standard.t: An LR-5 observation in an at-risk liver is hepatocellular carcinoma and this is the HCC pathway from here — including the transplant question, which that page opens.
standard.pref: Every LR-5 observation. 94% (95% CI 92-96) of pooled LR-5 observations were confirmed HCC and 97% (95-99) were confirmed malignant, which is what justifies treating without tissue in this population and nowhere else.
standard.avoid: 6% of pooled LR-5 observations were not HCC and 3% were not malignant, and the pooled data are retrospective with acknowledged verification and incorporation bias. The size of that bias has been measured: in a 43-study meta-analysis, the CT/MRI LR-5 HCC proportion was 92.3% where pathology was the reference standard against 97% where a composite imaging standard was used (p=0.01), and for LR-4 it was 63.4% against 81.2% (p=0.03) — so between 5 and 18 percentage points of the headline figures come from confirming HCC partly by its LR-5 appearance on another modality. LR-5 is not a histological diagnosis, and a lesion with an atypical clinical context deserves the board's attention before a treatment commitment. Downgraded from B to C for that reason.
standard.note: The local master workup CPG sets the staging bundle for this destination: multiphasic liver CT or MRI, chest CT, alpha-fetoprotein, and assessment of LI-RADS and OPTN class and vascular invasion, with biopsy only when imaging is atypical or a mixed or intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma diagnosis is suspected and the multidisciplinary team agrees.

standard.t: A targetoid or LR-M observation is a non-HCC malignancy until proved otherwise — route it to the iCCA pathway, and to the cHCC-CCA pathway where both phenotypes are present or the diagnosis is genuinely mixed.
standard.pref: Rim arterial hyperenhancement, peripheral washout, delayed central enhancement, an infiltrative pattern, marked diffusion restriction, or necrosis. 93% (95% CI 87-97) of pooled CT/MRI LR-M observations were malignant but only 36% (26-48) were HCC, which is precisely why the category exists and why it routes away from the HCC page.
standard.avoid: LR-M is not a diagnosis of cholangiocarcinoma, and on contrast-enhanced ultrasound the mix is different again — but less precisely than this page previously said. In a meta-analysis of 1,046 CEUS LR-M observations, 54% (44-65) were HCC and 40% (28-53) non-HCC malignancy, with heterogeneity of I-squared 84% and 88%; the widely quoted 94% malignant is the arithmetic sum of those two separately pooled proportions, carries no confidence interval anywhere, and does not match the raw counts, which give 1,011 of 1,046 or 96.7%. Removing a single case-control study moves the HCC proportion from 54% to 59% and halves the heterogeneity, 31% of the non-HCC malignancies have no specified diagnosis, and the non-HCC proportion is 35% in Asian and hepatitis-B-dominant studies against 54% in Western ones. The direction is reliable — a CEUS LR-M carries a materially higher chance of being HCC than a CT or MRI LR-M — and the numbers are not. Tissue decides, and gate 7 governs the route by which it is obtained. Note too the surgical position: no imaging feature is unique to intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma, so a peripherally enhancing mass in a non-cirrhotic liver cannot be called cholangiocarcinoma, metastasis or HCC on imaging alone.
standard.note: Washout timing is the practical discriminator at the scanner. In a 320-patient subanalysis, intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma showed early portal-venous washout in the tumour centre in 85.8% of cases against 49.8% for HCC, initial peripheral enhancement in 85.7% against 61%, and late-phase hypoenhancement in 92.9% against 75%; cirrhosis was present in 76.9% of the HCC patients and 16.7% of the cholangiocarcinoma patients. That subanalysis is one of the papers on this page still read from its abstract only. Downgraded from B to C.

standard.t: Route by primary where there is one: a confirmed colorectal primary is the CRLM pathway, a confirmed neuroendocrine primary is the NELM pathway, and a hepatocellular lesion in a normal liver that is not focal nodular hyperplasia is the HCA pathway.
standard.pref: As soon as the primary or the entity is established. Each destination page carries its own resectability criteria, its own sequencing and its own biopsy rules, and routing early is how those rules get applied rather than discovered late.
standard.avoid: Do not route on a presumption. The local CPG requires colorectal origin to be confirmed and the primary's resection and the absence of active extrahepatic disease to be verified before the CRLM destination, and requires central pathology review of grade and differentiation before the neuroendocrine one.
standard.note: Hepatic epithelioid haemangioendothelioma is in the programme's scope but has no page in this set; the local CPG requires expert pathology review for it because of diagnostic overlap, and it goes to the board as its own case.

alt.t: Where the lesion looks hepatocellular but the liver is normal and the patient is male, or the lesion is over 5 cm, route to the HCA pathway with those features stated rather than attempting to resolve the subtype here.
alt.pref: The hepatocellular lesion that is not focal nodular hyperplasia. The HCA pathway carries the 5 cm threshold, the male-sex indication and the subtype-specific risks; this page's job is to get the patient there with the right question attached.
alt.avoid: Do not discharge a hepatocellular lesion as focal nodular hyperplasia on hepatobiliary-phase uptake alone when the clinical context is wrong for it. Specificity against all adenoma subtypes together is 89% (95% CI 82-94), and 65% (44-80) against beta-catenin-activated and unclassified adenoma once the commoner subtypes have been excluded on conventional MRI — and 59% of beta-catenin-activated adenomas, the subtype with the highest malignant potential, take up the agent.
alt.note: Incidental adenoma is rare — 19 cases, 0.04%, in 45,319 hospital ultrasound examinations, with a mean confirmed size of 39.0 mm and confirmation required by CEUS, MRI or histology — so an incidental hepatocellular lesion that is not focal nodular hyperplasia deserves a second look at the history, particularly oestrogen and androgen exposure and glycogen storage disease. EASL's own figure for adenoma prevalence is 0.001-0.004%, three to four orders of magnitude lower, and neither document reconciles with the other.

alt.t: Where the lesion cannot be assigned to a single destination, send it to the board as an unassigned case with the competing possibilities named, rather than entering it on the closest-looking page.
alt.pref: The mass with both hepatocellular and cholangiocytic features, the discordant marker profile, the lesion whose phenotype changed between studies. The cHCC-CCA pathway exists for the first of these and should be named explicitly.
alt.avoid: Do not default to the HCC pathway because it is the busiest one. An LR-M observation treated as HCC is the error this gate exists to prevent, and the pooled CT/MRI LR-M HCC proportion is 36% (95% CI 26-48) — so most LR-M observations are malignancies that are not HCC, and the category routes accordingly.

avoid.t: Do not route a patient out of this page without a named destination, a named owner and a date.
avoid.pref: One destination page, one owner, one date, recorded in the conference note alongside the staging adequacy and the allocation classification, as the local CPG's minimum conference note requires.
avoid.avoid: A recommendation to 'refer to hepatobiliary' with no named destination is how a patient re-enters this pathway six months later at the same gate.

avoid.t: Do not discharge a patient from this page without telling them, in writing, what the lesion is and that no follow-up is needed.
avoid.pref: A discharge letter that names the entity, states the criteria it met, and says explicitly that no further imaging is required.
avoid.avoid: An unexplained benign finding is re-investigated by the next clinician who sees the report. The discharge rule only works if it is communicated.

quickref.intro: The fork at gate 0. Getting this wrong invalidates every category assigned downstream.

quickref.foot: EASL 2025 states that the non-invasive criteria should only be applied to patients with cirrhosis, chronic HBV infection or a history of HCC, and that in other patients the diagnosis of HCC should be confirmed by biopsy (LoE 1, strong recommendation, consensus), giving as its reason that the pre-test probability in those other populations has not been precisely established. It also states that LI-RADS should be preferred over the 2018 EASL algorithm because of the LR-M and LR-TIV refinements, while noting the two have similar performance for HCC (LoE 3). LI-RADS v2018 itself excludes patients under 18 and cirrhosis due to congenital hepatic fibrosis or to vascular disorders, and its own authors state that nothing in the system licenses applying a category outside the at-risk population, because every probability in it was derived under high HCC prevalence. The two agent recommendations point in opposite directions because they answer different questions; the request form must say which question is being asked. The two ACR documents define risk differently, which a pathway using both has to reconcile — this page forks on liver disease first, at gate 0.

Nonrim APHE, 20 mm or more
0 LR-4 · 1 or more LR-5
LR-M
Targetoid — rim APHE, peripheral washout, delayed central enhancement — or nontargetoid: infiltrative, marked diffusion restriction, necrosis

Management, LR-4
Multidisciplinary discussion; shorter-interval imaging or biopsy

Treat as HCC / obtain tissue, route to the iCCA or cHCC-CCA pathway
Which major features carry the weight
Nonperipheral washout OR 13.2 (9.0-19.2) · nonrim APHE OR 10.3 (6.7-15.6) · enhancing capsule OR 2.4 (1.7-3.5) · threshold growth OR 1.6 (0.8-3.4), not associated
Interreader agreement, major features
APHE and washout kappa 0.84-0.87 · capsule controversial, excellent in one study and not in the others

All included studies were retrospective and observation selection was the most frequent source of bias through verification bias and case-control design, so these are not calibrated to an unselected incidental population, and the authors label the LR-2 estimate provisional and at high risk of bias. A 43-study meta-analysis quantifies the reference-standard effect: the LR-5 HCC proportion is 92.3% with pathology against 97% with a composite imaging standard, and LR-4 63.4% against 81.2%. Two further cautions. The 2022 individual-patient-data meta-analysis of 5,364 observations shows the four major features are not equivalent — washout and arterial hyperenhancement carry the diagnosis, capsule contributes weakly and reached significance in only one of three analysis cohorts, and threshold growth was not associated with HCC at all, assessable in only 452 of 4,434 observations and reported with two different confidence intervals in the same paper, whose online version was corrected in February 2023. And agreement on the output that drives management is much worse than agreement on the features: kappa 0.30-0.39 for CEUS categories against 0.84-0.87 for the features themselves, which means the same lesion can receive different categories from two readers or on two modalities. The v2018 change was narrow — the threshold-growth definition was simplified to align with AASLD and OPTN, and 10-19 mm observations with nonrim APHE plus nonperipheral washout became LR-5. CEUS LI-RADS remains at v2017 and its categories are not interchangeable: 97% (95-98) of CEUS LR-5 observations were HCC, CEUS LR-3 is 21% HCC against 35% for CT/MRI LR-3, and CEUS LR-M is 54% HCC against 36%. The two CEUS meta-analyses behind those figures come from the same department with overlapping studies and are not independent. Verify the table against the current ACR core document before clinical use.

Benign features: no workup. Suspicious or flash-filling: prompt MRI

MRI in 3 to 6 months, to characterise and assess growth

Benign features: no MRI. Suspicious or flash-filling: prompt MRI

Benign features

Suspicious features

quickref.foot: The four core recommendations are: forgo workup of lesions under 1 cm in low-risk patients; forgo workup of lesions with distinctly benign features regardless of risk; pursue workup of lesions 1 cm or larger lacking benign features in high-risk patients; and use MRI for further workup. Read the document's own disclaimers, because they are stronger than the way it is usually cited: the committee states that its consensus processes meet ACR policy standards but do not meet any specific formal national standards, that the product is not an ACR Practice Guideline or Appropriateness Criteria policy, that it should be termed guidance rather than guidelines, and that its content must be viewed as recommendations and should not be considered standard of care. It was finalised by informal iterative consensus by five abdominal radiologists, one hepatologist and one hepatobiliary surgeon, with no systematic review, no search strategy, no evidence tables and no grading of evidence anywhere. Every threshold in it is a convention: 1 cm, 1.5 cm, 3 cm, 20 HU, 3-6 months, 1 year of stability, none derived and none validated, and four of them changed from the 2010 version without new evidence. The benign and suspicious feature lists carry no interobserver agreement data, and the 20 HU rule is acknowledged to be unreliable in the sub-centimetre lesions that make up most of the caseload. The opening claim that incidental liver lesions are found in up to 30% of individuals over 40 is a block citation of nineteen heterogeneous references with no pooled estimate behind it. Flash filling means uniform enhancement relative to parenchyma on arterial-phase imaging; in cirrhosis the white paper notes most small wedge-shaped hypervascular lesions remain benign. The algorithm explicitly does not apply when the index CT was requested to evaluate a known liver abnormality, and was not designed for hepatic infection or abscess. The companion ACR Appropriateness Criteria topic, Liver Lesion-Initial Characterization, new in 2020, rates FDG PET-CT usually appropriate in only one of its eight variants, and its ratings are panel medians from a RAND/UCLA process whose dispersion and evidence grading are published only on a separate ACR website.

quickref.title: The four prevalence figures, and what each one counted
quickref.intro: Every one of these numbers is quoted as though it were the prior probability for an incidental liver lesion. None of them is. Use the figure whose denominator matches your patient, or quote none.
rows: Karhunen 1986 — 52%
49 of 95 consecutive forensic autopsies of Finnish men aged 35-69, with each liver sliced into 1-2 cm sections and 505 targeted blocks taken from suspect areas
What was inside that 52%

Bile duct microhamartomas and adenomas pooled, 26 men (27%), mean diameter 1.3 mm, range 0.3-4.5 mm · cavernous haemangioma 19 (20%), mean 5.2 mm · FNH 3 (3%) · adenoma 1 (1%). Nothing at 1.3 mm is visible on CT

254 of 1,454 consecutive outpatient contrast-enhanced abdominal CT examinations at one tertiary centre in 1989-90, on 10 mm contiguous non-helical sections. A per-examination rate, and 82% of those with lesions had a known cancer
What happened to those 254

129 (51%) judged benign, 55 (22%) malignant, 70 (27%) never resolved. Benignity rested on biopsy or imaging in 16 of 254 (6%) and on CT stability alone in the rest. Of the 45 patients with no known cancer, none had a malignant lesion — but 23 of the 45 had under 6 months of follow-up
Schwartz 1999 — 12.7%

378 of 2,978 cancer patients at one cancer centre in whom a radiology report mentioned a lesion 1 cm or smaller, or called one too small to characterise. A report-mention rate, from patients required to have had both an initial and a follow-up CT at the same institution
What happened to those 378

44 (11.6%) grew and were counted metastatic · 303 (80.2%) stable over a mean 25.6 months · 31 (8.2%) stable under 6 months and left indeterminate. Counting the indeterminates as malignant gives 19.8%, splitting them evenly 15.7%. No histology in any case
Kaltenbach 2016 — 15.1%

6,851 of 45,319 ultrasound examinations at one German university hospital over 11 years with at least one of five pre-specified benign findings. Metastases, HCC, cholangiocarcinoma, abscess and biliary hamartoma were never in the numerator
What was inside that 15.1%

Focal fatty sparing 2,839 (6.26%), a pseudolesion · simple cysts 2,631 (5.81%), not tumours — together four fifths of the total · haemangioma 1,640 (3.62% in the results table, printed as 3.3% in the abstract) · FNH 81 (0.18%) · adenoma 19 (0.04%). Solid benign tumours are under 4%
Gore 2017 — 'up to 30% over 40'

A block citation of nineteen references with no pooled estimate and no indication of which contributes what — autopsy series, CT colonography cohorts, lumbar spine MRI series, emergency CT reviews and cancer-surveillance series among them. There is no study behind the 30%
Are any of the four comparable

No. A targeted-autopsy rate in 95 men, a per-examination CT rate in cancer-surveillance outpatients, a report-mention rate in cancer patients who survived to a second scan, and a five-finding sonographic rate in hospital attenders. They resemble each other by coincidence
quickref.foot: The practical reading has not changed: on the fortuitous discovery of a liver lesion, first consideration goes to focal fatty sparing, a simple cyst and a haemangioma, and the finding of a focal nodular hyperplasia or an adenoma is rarely a random discovery. What has changed after the full-text read is that no single number may be quoted as the prior probability. Each figure fails as a prior for a different reason. Karhunen's 52% measures search intensity at targeted autopsy in a population selected for violent, cardiovascular and intoxication-related death — 49.5% cardiovascular, 15.8% intoxication, 1% neoplastic — and half of it is millimetre-scale lesions that no scanner will ever show; its clinically relevant numerators are 3 cases of FNH and 1 adenoma, for which a 1-in-95 estimate carries an interval of roughly 0 to 6%. Jones's 17% is an artefact of case mix in scans ordered to look for metastases, on a detection threshold set by 1989 technology, with benign and malignant both defined by whether the lesion grew on the same test. Schwartz's 12.7% measures how often a radiologist wrote a phrase, and its cohort is conditioned on surviving and returning for a second scan, which preferentially removes the patients whose lesions would have grown. Kaltenbach's 15.1% is the prevalence of five chosen benign findings, four fifths of it pseudolesion and cyst, in a university hospital population, with malignancy never in the numerator — so it cannot speak to the probability that a given lesion is benign, which is the only question a pathway asks. Three further details worth carrying. Kaltenbach's FNH figure of 0.18% and adenoma figure of 0.04% are roughly tenfold below every prior series, most plausibly because those two entities alone required confirmation by CEUS, MRI or histology while the three common findings were accepted on B-mode; mean confirmed sizes were 51.6 mm and 39.0 mm, so what was measured is the prevalence of large FNH and large adenoma. The same paper gives two different values for its own headline, 15.1% with n=6,839 in the abstract and n=6,851 in the results, and two for haemangioma, 3.3% and 3.62%. And the 11.6% that gets quoted from Schwartz is the most favourable of three analyses the authors ran; the upper one, 19.8%, is in the same table.

honest.t: This page is a first draft, revised once. There is no ratified Memorial Hermann or UTHealth roadmap for the incidental liver mass, and no institutional decision has been taken on anything in it except where the local Master Workup and Staging CPG is quoted directly.
honest.why: The only local document behind this page is that CPG, which is itself a draft for institutional review and is effective only after its approval block is completed. Every interval, threshold and discharge rule here is drawn from a published guideline or from the primary literature, and every one of them is a proposal to the group rather than a position the group holds. The second pass, on 7 October 2026, replaced numbers taken from abstracts with numbers from the full texts, added their confidence intervals, and downgraded fifteen evidence strings; it did not remove any recommendation.

honest.t: The at-risk fork at gate 0 is treated as binary. In practice a substantial number of patients sit between the two arms — advanced fibrosis without established cirrhosis, MASLD with a nodular liver, long-standing alcohol use with normal synthetic function.
honest.why: Neither LI-RADS nor EASL 2025 defines what to do with these patients, and EASL says only that the pre-test probability in non-cirrhotic populations has not been precisely established. The page's rule — name the uncertainty and treat the pathway as undetermined — is grade D and is an operating convention, not a finding.

honest.t: The follow-up interval for a regenerative or focal-nodular-hyperplasia-like nodule in a liver with a vascular disorder is not stated on this page because no guideline states one.
honest.why: LI-RADS excludes these livers from its population, and EASL's benign-tumour guideline withdraws its own no-follow-up rule for focal nodular hyperplasia in this setting without replacing it with an interval. Setting an interval is a local decision and belongs in the approvals list, not in a gate. The relevant EASL vascular-liver guidance on this page is the 2015 edition, which has since been superseded.

honest.t: Biliary hamartomas are discharged on this page with no interval, and that is an inference rather than a demonstrated safe practice.
honest.why: No surveillance interval is established, which is not the same as surveillance having been shown unnecessary. The association between von Meyenburg complexes and cholangiocarcinoma rests on roughly 35 case reports accumulated over about fifty years, set against an autopsy carrier prevalence of about 5.6% from a single 1996 series of 2,843 autopsies — which implies an absolute risk so small that nobody has computed it, and the reporting mechanism is itself the bias, since a complex that never causes trouble is not publishable. The molecular evidence of neoplastic potential is loss-of-heterozygosity analysis in two patients and a Ki-67 gradient in a four-case series. Discharging them is reasonable and is what everyone does; it is not evidence based, and the imaging recommendation that supports the diagnosis carries no accuracy data at all.

honest.t: The position that a resectable lesion you intend to resect should not be biopsied is stated on this page as one rule, but the evidence behind it differs by an order of magnitude between diseases.
honest.why: For colorectal liver metastases the track-deposit rate was 19% in a retrospective series of 90 patients biopsied at referring hospitals, with a 14.2% absolute 4-year survival difference whose interval runs from 2.0% to 26.4%, a 61%-against-26% imbalance in synchronous disease and an adjusted analysis reported only as a p-value from the wrong statistical test; for hepatocellular carcinoma a meta-analysis of 8 observational studies put seeding at 2.7% (1.8-4.0) per patient, or 0.9% per patient per year, with the largest and only prospective study reporting zero events in 239 patients; for perihilar cholangiocarcinoma the figure everyone cites rests on 6 patients. Presenting these as one position is a simplification the page makes deliberately, and the group should decide whether to keep it.

honest.t: The ACR white paper's recommendation to use gadoxetate disodium to separate focal nodular hyperplasia from adenoma has been materially weakened since 2017 — and this page previously stated the weakening in the wrong terms.
honest.why: The 2022 meta-analysis of 28 studies and 410 subtyped adenomas found hepatobiliary-phase iso- or hyperintensity in 59% (95% CI 26-88%) of beta-catenin-activated adenomas. Specificity for separating focal nodular hyperplasia from all adenoma subtypes together is 89% (82-94%); the 65% (44-80%) figure applies only once HNF1A-inactivated and inflammatory adenomas have been excluded, so it is the specificity against the residual enriched population rather than the performance of the test on an unselected lesion. The earlier draft of this page quoted 65% as the specificity without that condition, which overstated the problem. What survives is still decisive for the discharge rule: 33 beta-catenin-activated adenomas spread across 28 studies, 16 of them case reports or small series, cannot support a point estimate; the paired sensitivities of 99% carry intervals of 57-100% and 53-100%; all four diagnostic-performance studies were case-control and marked high risk of bias for patient selection; and the hepatobiliary phase could not separate beta-catenin-activated from inflammatory adenoma, the commonest subtype of all.

honest.t: The LI-RADS category malignancy probabilities quoted throughout this page should not be read as applying to an unselected incidental population.
honest.why: Every study in the pooled analysis was retrospective, observation selection was the commonest source of bias through verification bias and case-control design, and the pooled cohort was about 70% HCC by observation. The system's own authors state that LI-RADS applies only to patients with or at risk for HCC, and that every probability in it was derived under high HCC prevalence. An incidental lesion in a cirrhotic liver found on a scan done for something else has a lower prior than an observation entered into a LI-RADS validation study, so the LR-3 and LR-4 figures in particular are likely overestimates here — and outside the at-risk population they are not estimates of anything. The reference standard adds a measurable inflation of its own: LR-5 reads 92.3% HCC against pathology and 97% against a composite imaging standard.

honest.t: No evidence quantifies how often a liver lesion that appears on one modality and not on another proves malignant, and this page does not pretend otherwise.
honest.why: Targeted searching returns nothing. The reconciliation step at gate 6 — compare the images rather than the reports, check phase timing, coverage, dose and breath-hold — is mechanistic reasoning plus a local failure pattern, graded D. What is documented is only that 6.8% of lesions unclear on greyscale ultrasound remained undiagnosed after a standardised contrast-enhanced ultrasound in a 1,349-patient multicentre study, and that most of those were benign.

honest.t: Contrast-enhanced ultrasound is presented on this page as a characterising test, and its specificity for a benign diagnosis is the weak half of its performance.
honest.why: In the DEGUM multicentre study, sensitivity for malignancy was 95.8% but specificity was 83.1%, and in the companion analysis 8 lesions called benign by contrast-enhanced ultrasound proved malignant — three HCCs called adenoma, two called focal nodular hyperplasia, two called haemangioma, one called benign that was lymphoma. Those are the exact errors a triage page is designed to prevent, and they happened in a 14-centre study using a standardised protocol with histology as the reference standard in more than 75% of cases.

honest.t: The discharge rules on this page assume a competent index study. In a patient whose CT was dose-reduced, single-phase, or did not cover the segment, none of the benign-feature rules can be applied, and the page does not say what happens then beyond 'order the right study'.
honest.why: The ACR white paper itself warns that assessing small liver lesions is challenging when aggressive dose-reduction has been used, particularly in high-risk patients, without defining adequacy, and separately concedes that in a lesion under 1 cm an accurate attenuation measurement may not be attainable at all — which is the measurement the 20 HU benign-feature rule depends on. It also recommends eliminating the unenhanced phase whenever possible, while its own benign-feature definition rests on non-contrast attenuation. What counts as an adequate study for the purpose of discharging a lesion is a local imaging-standards question and has no published answer.

honest.t: The cystic gate names mucinous cystic neoplasm as a surgical lesion on the basis of surgical series with no denominator.
honest.why: Grade D. The best available support is a six-case report from one Karachi pathology file in which every lesion had been operated on under a preoperative impression of simple or hydatid cyst, recurrence occurred in three of the five patients with any follow-up, margins could not be assessed in at least three of six because specimens arrived opened or in pieces, no dysplasia or malignancy was found in any case, and the 20% malignant-transformation figure invoked to justify radical resection is a single citation with no denominator. The authors attribute their recurrence rate partly to limited local hepatobiliary surgical expertise. There is no comparative evidence for resection over observation in a radiologically suspected mucinous cystic neoplasm, no study establishes how often a septated cystic liver lesion is one, and the septation sign is contradicted by the series' own figure legend.

honest.t: The tumour board operating model and the metrics below are reproduced from the programme's standard pattern so that one operating standard covers every liver pathway. They are grade D by construction and should be audited for adherence, not for effectiveness.
honest.why: They are stakeholder-derived operating requirements, labelled standard because the programme chooses them, not because any trial supports them. The local Master Workup and Staging CPG supplies the specific steps — the safety screen, central imaging and pathology review, the disposition categories and the minimum conference note — and is itself a draft pending approval.

honest.t: The four prevalence figures this page used to quote side by side are not comparable, and the page no longer quotes any single number as the prior probability for an incidental liver lesion.
honest.why: Karhunen's 52% is 95 forensic autopsies of Finnish men aged 35-69 with targeted sectioning, half of it bile-duct microhamartomas of mean diameter 1.3 mm — nothing visible on any scanner. Jones's 17% is a per-examination rate in 1,454 outpatient contrast CTs in 1989-90, 82% of them with known cancer, on 10 mm non-helical sections. Schwartz's 12.7% is a radiology-report mention rate in cancer patients required to have had two or more CTs at the same centre, which conditions the cohort on survival and removes the patients whose lesions would have grown. Kaltenbach's 15.1% counts five pre-specified benign findings in 45,319 hospital ultrasound examinations, four fifths of it focal fatty sparing and simple cysts, with malignancy never in the numerator. One is an autopsy rate, one a per-examination rate, one a report-mention rate and one a five-finding sonographic rate; they resemble one another by coincidence. The quick reference now carries each with its denominator.

honest.t: The 'up to 30% of individuals older than 40' figure that opens the ACR white paper, and that every local pathway inherits, has no study behind it.
honest.why: It is supported by a block citation of nineteen references with no indication of which contributes what. Those nineteen include a 45,319-patient ultrasound series, a cancer-surveillance CT series, CT colonography screening cohorts, lumbar spine MRI series, emergency abdominal CT reviews and a renal-colic series — incompatible denominators and incompatible lesion definitions, with no pooled estimate anywhere. It is a round number standing in for a literature that ranges from under 4% to 52% depending on what was counted and how hard anyone looked.

honest.t: The ACR Incidental Findings Committee states that its own consensus process meets no specific formal national standard and that its recommendations are not standard of care — and this page is built on it.
honest.why: The committee writes that its processes meet ACR policy standards but do not meet any specific formal national standards, that the product is not an ACR Practice Guideline or Appropriateness Criteria policy, that it should be termed guidance rather than guidelines, and that its content should not be considered standard of care, with radiologists free to deviate. There is no systematic review, no search strategy, no evidence tables and no grading anywhere in it. The thresholds behave accordingly: between 2010 and 2017 the risk tiers went from three to two, the small-lesion stratum from 0.5 cm to 1 cm, the follow-up interval from 6 months to 3-6 months, the focal-nodular-hyperplasia threshold from 4 cm to 3 cm, and quoted biopsy morbidity from 2.0-4.8% to 0.5%, with no new evidence cited for any of it and the same subcommittee chair on both documents. The founding 2010 paper also records the committee's own hypothesis that academic radiologists may be biased toward imaging overuse and that its guidance might not reduce utilisation or could increase it.

honest.t: LI-RADS category assignment is much less reproducible than the features it is built from, so the category a patient receives depends in part on who read the study and on which scanner they entered.
honest.why: Interreader agreement for arterial phase hyperenhancement and washout is excellent at kappa 0.84-0.87, and that is the figure the system's own report leads with. Agreement on the category that drives management is fair for CEUS at kappa 0.30-0.39, fair to substantial for MRI at 0.35-0.61, and substantial for CT at 0.79; agreement for the capsule feature is described by the same report as controversial, excellent in one study and not in the others; and intermodality agreement is kappa 0.33-0.39 between CT and MRI and 0.22 between MRI and CEUS, with CT tending to undercategorise. The report states all of this and treats none of it as a problem requiring resolution. This page therefore puts the category in the report and sends LR-3 and LR-4 to the board rather than to an algorithm.

honest.t: Two of the four LI-RADS major features are not carrying the diagnostic weight the table implies, and the paper that showed this cannot give stable effect sizes.
honest.why: In an individual-patient-data meta-analysis of 5,364 observations from 32 studies, nonperipheral washout and nonrim arterial hyperenhancement had odds ratios of 13.2 (95% CI 9.0-19.2) and 10.3 (6.7-15.6), while enhancing capsule was only 2.4 (1.7-3.5) and reached significance in just one of three analysis cohorts, and threshold growth was not associated with HCC at all. The threshold-growth result is reported twice in the same article with different intervals and p-values, OR 1.6 (0.8-3.4), p=0.19 and OR 1.6 (0.7-3.6), p=0.07, and the online version carries a correction notice. It was assessable in only 452 of 4,434 observations, missing mostly because prior imaging did not exist — so the one cohort that could test it is the least representative. Several odds ratios invert direction between analysis cohorts, 78% of contributing studies were at high risk of bias, and only 32 of 81 eligible studies shared data, by author willingness. The page keeps the v2018 table because it is the current system, and says here that its components are unequal.

honest.t: The two contrast-enhanced ultrasound meta-analyses this page uses are not independent corroboration of each other.
honest.why: Both come from the same ultrasound department in Tianjin, share authors, share the same four funding grants, draw on overlapping included studies and were published two months apart in 2022. They also disagree: one reports CEUS LR-M as 44% HCC and the other as 56%, from largely the same primary literature, without either acknowledging the other's estimate. A third meta-analysis from a separate group gives 54% (95% CI 44-65). Heterogeneity across all three is I-squared 78-95%, the LR-3 HCC proportion moves from 14% in Asian to 32% in non-Asian studies, and the widely quoted figure that 94% of CEUS LR-M lesions are malignant is the arithmetic sum of two separately pooled proportions with no confidence interval anywhere. Citing two of these papers as agreeing is counting one body of work twice.

honest.t: The prospective evidence that contrast-enhanced ultrasound resolves an indeterminate CT or MRI observation comes from a 97% cirrhotic cohort and licenses nothing about a non-cirrhotic incidental mass.
honest.why: In the only prospective primary study behind this page, 75 observations in 68 patients were re-assessed by CEUS after CT or MRI had returned LR-3 or non-characterizable. The cohort was 97.1% cirrhotic, 23.5% had a personal history of HCC, and every patient was enrolled because a lesion had already been found on surveillance; at that prevalence a CT/MRI LR-3 observation carried a 25.9% HCC risk and a non-characterizable one 52.4%. The reported 100% positive and negative predictive values rest on 7, 7, 6 and 1 observations with no confidence interval printed anywhere in the paper — 7 of 7 has an exact interval of roughly 59-100%. Readers could see the prior CT or MRI in most cases, the reference standard was follow-up CT or MRI in 72% of observations, persistently indeterminate nodules at one year were counted non-malignant, CEUS left 74.1% of LR-3 observations still indeterminate, the sub-analysis was not the basis of the parent trial's sample size, and the study was funded in part by the manufacturer of the contrast agent. Nothing in it transfers to a lesion in a liver that is not at risk.

honest.t: The ACR Appropriateness Criteria call contrast-enhanced ultrasound, multiphase CT and contrast-enhanced MRI equivalent for an indeterminate lesion over 1 cm, and the same document cites specificity for one of them as low as 38%.
honest.why: The equivalence is asserted on narrative accuracy ranges from different studies in different populations, with no head-to-head data, no pooled estimates and no formal equivalence testing; the ranges actually cited are wide enough to contain clinically important differences, including contrast-enhanced CT specificity of 38-82% in ultrasound-detected lesions and one MRI study at 43% specificity for an exact diagnosis. The ratings are panel medians from a RAND/UCLA process whose rating dispersion and GRADE assessment are published on a separate ACR website rather than in the paper, so a reader cannot tell which ratings were near-unanimous and which were marginal — only one variant carries an explicit disagreement label. Several procedures are rated usually not appropriate on the stated basis that no relevant literature supports their use, which converts absence of evidence into a numerical rating. The document also redefines the risk categories incompatibly with the white paper from the same organisation. And its 1 cm variant boundary is inherited without derivation, in a document that gives no accuracy data stratified by size.

honest.t: Procedural harm figures for liver biopsy differ by an order of magnitude across the sources this page relies on, and none of them is for the procedure a patient would actually have.
honest.why: The ACR white paper gives morbidity of about 0.5% and mortality about 0.05%; the same committee's 2010 document gave 2.0-4.8% morbidity with no explanation for the revision. The AASLD position paper gives severe bleeding at 1 in 2,500 to 1 in 10,000 and mortality at about 1 in 10,000, but states explicitly that these are for the intercostal percutaneous approach in diffuse non-focal parenchymal disease, and notes in one clause that death from bleeding may be greater after biopsy of a malignant lesion; its seeding figure of 0.13% is twenty-fold below the 2.7% pooled for hepatocellular carcinoma. For endoscopic ultrasound-guided fine-needle biopsy, a meta-analysis of 99 studies and 9,303 patients puts the overall adverse-event rate at 1.8% but the liver subgroup at 14.0% (95% CI 7.7-24.0) — on 133 patients in 4 studies with 18 events, of which 13 were abdominal pain, 3 were bleeds and one was a suspected death that the paper's conclusion denies occurred; the serious-event rate, which the paper never states, is about 3%. The same review found prospective studies reporting 60% more adverse events than retrospective ones, which means the reassuring overall figure is an under-ascertainment. The page therefore quotes a range and names the route.

honest.t: The EASL vascular-liver guidance this page cites is the 2015 edition and has been superseded by a 2026 edition that was not obtained for this page.
honest.why: Every statement on this page sourced to that document — the Budd-Chiari nodule prevalence of 60-80%, the 4% cumulative HCC incidence at a median 5 years, the biopsy triggers for a Budd-Chiari nodule, and the scope rule that these livers are managed outside the HCC algorithms — comes from a guideline built on the agenda of a single 2012 conference, with a PubMed-only search, no search string or date limits, and committee opinion where evidence was absent. It never reports the inverse probability a radiologist needs, which is the chance of underlying vascular disease given multiple hypervascular nodules in a non-cirrhotic liver. A 2026 EASL edition exists and this page has not read it, so the whole of gate 0's vascular arm and gate 5's alternative column are provisional pending that read. Obtaining it is an approvals item.

honest.t: Nodular regenerative hyperplasia has been reclassified as a marker of a vascular disorder rather than a benign nodular tumour, and the consensus that did it describes its own diagnostic score as unvalidated.
honest.why: The 2026 multisociety consensus on porto-sinusoidal vascular disorder or non-cirrhotic portal fibrosis makes nodular regenerative hyperplasia one of three major histological criteria for the disorder, alongside muscularised portal venules and portal venule stenosis in 50% or more of portal tracts, and makes liver biopsy mandatory for the diagnosis. Read what it does not establish. The criteria were derived in 88 European patients who all had specific signs of portal hypertension, while the definition permits diagnosis in patients without portal hypertension — which is exactly the patient an incidental nodular liver produces. A major criterion qualifies on a sensitivity of 0.10 provided specificity exceeds 0.95, so the framework is built for ruling in and the sensitivity of the whole criterion set is never stated. Specificity was tested against 41 normal donors and 89 chronic-liver-disease controls that deliberately excluded biliary disease. The diagnostic score was built by converting votes on 36 hypothetical scenarios into weights and then shown to reproduce those votes, which is arithmetic consistency, not diagnostic validity; no patient was classified by it in the paper. The term in the title carried 74% agreement against a pre-specified 75% threshold. And the consensus says nothing about how incidentally detected nodular regenerative hyperplasia should be handled, nor what proportion of it represents the disorder.

honest.t: The abscess drainage recommendation on this page does not hold in the size range in which most abscesses present, and the safety claim behind it is not a safety claim.
honest.why: In the pooled analysis of 12 randomised trials, the confidence interval for catheter drainage over needle aspiration crossed the line of no effect in the 5-10 cm subgroup — which is 8 of the 12 trials and the commonest clinical scenario — while excluding it only in the >5 cm and >10 cm strata, three trials between them; the abstract nonetheless states that the subgroups confirmed the consistency of the benefit, which is true of the direction of the point estimates and not of significance. Nine of 12 trials were Indian and 8 enrolled mixed amoebic-predominant abscesses, so pyogenic abscess rests on 3 trials and 212 patients with no separate pooled estimate reported. 'Clinical treatment success' is never defined, and the authors name varying definitions as the likely source of the 56% heterogeneity. The complication odds ratio of 1.02 comes from 7 of the 12 trials with an interval of 0.30-3.50, which permits a 70% reduction or a 3.5-fold increase and is uninformative rather than reassuring. Catheter drainage remains this page's recommendation; the pooled odds ratio of 4.12 is a direction, not a threshold, and there is no size below which a single aspiration has been shown sufficient.

honest.t: MRI is not better than CT for a liver lesion in a cancer patient except below 10 mm, and below 10 mm it still misses two metastases in five.
honest.why: In the meta-analysis of 39 prospective studies and 3,391 treatment-naive colorectal cancer patients, per-lesion sensitivity was 80.3% for MRI against 74.4% for CT with overlapping intervals, and per-patient sensitivity 88.2% against 83.6%, p=0.653 — neither significant. The only significant advantage was below 10 mm, 60.2% against 47.3%, p=0.006, and at 10 mm or larger there was no difference at all. The earlier draft of this page presented both the per-lesion and per-patient figures as MRI outperforming CT, which they do not. Three negative findings in the same paper also restrain protocol claims that are often made: multisection CT was no better than single-section, dual-phase no better than portal-phase alone, and liver-specific contrast agents gave no measurable benefit. The uncomfortable consequence for gate 6 is that the test the algorithm sends a sub-centimetre lesion to has a sensitivity of 60% at that size, in a staging population with a far higher prior than an incidental one.

honest.t: Several documents this page relies on were read only as abstracts or guideline text and not in full, and their numbers have not been checked against a full text.
honest.why: The full-text read of 7 October 2026 covered thirty papers. It did not cover the EASL hepatocellular carcinoma guideline of 2025, the AASLD practice guidance of 2023, the three DEGUM contrast-enhanced ultrasound papers (the 1,349-patient multicentre study, its unclear-lesion companion and the 320-patient HCC-versus-cholangiocarcinoma subanalysis), the perihilar fine-needle aspiration series, or the fatty-liver imaging review. Every figure on this page attributed to those six sources is therefore at the same evidentiary standard as the first draft, including the DEGUM sensitivity and specificity of 95.8% and 83.1%, the washout-timing percentages at gate 8, and the 5-of-6 perihilar figure at gate 7. Two further documents named in the gap scan were sought and not obtained: the 2026 EASL vascular-liver guideline and the CAMINO study. Neither is cited here as read.

board: Submission — an Epic form captures the index study and its protocol adequacy, whether the liver is at risk and on what basis, any known extrahepatic primary, lesion number and size, the imaging phenotype and LI-RADS category where one applies, prior imaging available for comparison, the specific question being asked, the referring clinician and the urgency. Owner: submitting clinician.

Triage — a coordinator and a clinically trained gatekeeper check whether the case is a decision question at all. A large share of incidental liver lesions are resolved by the radiologist against the ACR algorithm and never need the board; the triage step exists to protect agenda time for the lesions that fork the pathway. Owners: coordinator and chair.

Safety screen — suspected perihilar cholangiocarcinoma is flagged before any primary-tumour biopsy, as the local Master Workup and Staging CPG requires; active infection, biliary sepsis, renal dysfunction, decompensation and pregnancy are flagged at the same step. Owner: coordinator with the transplant hepatology on-call.

Central imaging review — transplant and diagnostic radiology review the index study and all priors together, in DICOM, before any recommendation. Reports are not reviewed in place of images. Where the protocol was inadequate, the team documents whether repeat imaging is required before selection. Owner: diagnostic radiology.
Agenda — stable at least 24 hours ahead. Incidental cases are grouped so that the at-risk and not-at-risk arms are discussed as separate blocks, because the criteria differ. Owner: coordinator.

Attendance — diagnostic radiology, hepatobiliary and transplant surgery, hepatology, medical oncology, interventional radiology and pathology are required for this pathway; advanced endoscopy attends when a biliary lesion is on the list. Owners: specialty leads.

Pathology — pre-alerted for every case in which a biopsy is contemplated, with tissue priorities agreed before the procedure in the CPG's order: diagnostic confirmation, required biomarkers, broad sequencing, research, and tumour-informed circulating-tumour-DNA assay creation. Owner: pathology.

Output — one of four dispositions, named explicitly: discharge with no follow-up; a defined interval with a named owner and date; tissue, with the route agreed; or routing to a named destination pathway. 'Refer to hepatobiliary' is not a disposition. Owner: chair.

Discharge communication — where the disposition is discharge, a letter to the patient and the referrer naming the entity, the criteria it met and the explicit statement that no further imaging is required. Owner: named owner.

Documentation — an Epic note within one business day, in the CPG's minimum conference note format: diagnosis, stage, date of last complete staging, resectability and alternative-curative assessment, protocol eligibility and deviations, allocation classification where relevant, and the decision with its conditions, interval and accountable owner. Owner: named owner.
Registry — the case closed with the index modality, the risk category, the final entity, the disposition, and whether the pathway ended in discharge, routing or tissue. Owner: coordinator.
Referring relationships — the referring clinician is told the entity and who owns the next step. This pathway returns patients with an answer; it does not capture them. Owner: named owner.
dashboard: Proportion of incidental liver lesions discharged at the index report against the ACR algorithm, without a board discussion or a follow-up interval (§approvals 1).
Follow-up intervals recommended for lesions meeting ACR benign-feature criteria — the measure of unnecessary surveillance generated by this pathway.
MRI agent used, the question stated on the request, and whether the study answered it (§approvals 3).
FDG PET-CT ordered for liver lesion characterisation, by lesion size and risk category, against the single ACR Appropriateness Criteria variant that supports it (§approvals 4).
Biopsies performed on lesions that were subsequently resected, and biopsies performed on patients with resectable colorectal liver metastases (§approvals 5).
Biopsy route documented for every cholangiocarcinoma candidate, as the local CPG requires, and any primary-tumour biopsy performed before transplant-pathway review — a reportable safety event.
Interval-adherence: deferred lesions re-imaged within the recommended window, with a named owner recorded at the time the interval was set.
Cases routed to a named destination pathway within one board cycle of the entity being established, by destination.
Final entity against the index imaging impression, for every case that reached tissue or resection — the pathway's own diagnostic accuracy.
Cryptogenic pyogenic liver abscesses in which a search for an occult hepatobiliary or colorectal cancer was completed during the index admission (§approvals 7).
Registry closure: index modality, risk category, final entity and disposition recorded for every case.
Reports or patient letters quoting a prevalence figure for benign liver lesions without naming its population (§approvals 11).
LI-RADS categories that changed between modalities or between readers, and whether the disposition changed with them (§approvals 12).
Biopsy route recorded for every liver biopsy, with complications by route (§approvals 14).

approvals.q: Which incidental liver lesions may be discharged by the radiologist at the index report without any clinical referral, and which must be referred?
approvals.why: The ACR algorithm is explicit that lesions under 1 cm in low-risk patients and lesions with distinctly benign features in any patient need no workup, but it is a radiology consensus document and it does not say who owns the discharge. Without a local rule, either every finding generates a referral or none does.
approvals.audit: Proportion discharged at the index report; follow-up intervals recommended for lesions meeting benign-feature criteria.

approvals.q: How is the at-risk question answered and recorded when cirrhosis is suspected but not established?
approvals.why: The whole algorithm forks here, and neither LI-RADS nor EASL 2025 defines the intermediate patient. EASL states only that pre-test probability in non-cirrhotic populations has not been precisely established.
approvals.audit: Cases in which the at-risk determination was changed after the index report, and the reason.

approvals.q: Which MRI contrast agent is the default when the question has not been narrowed?
approvals.why: EASL 2025 favours extracellular agents over gadoxetic acid for the HCC question (LoE 1, strong), while the ACR white paper recommends gadoxetate specifically for focal nodular hyperplasia versus adenoma. The two cannot be satisfied in one acquisition, and the 65% specificity figure against β-catenin-activated and unclassified adenoma weakens the second recommendation substantially since 2017.
approvals.audit: Agent used, question stated on the request, and whether a repeat study with the other agent was subsequently needed.

approvals.q: May FDG PET-CT be ordered for liver lesion characterisation from the radiology report alone?
approvals.why: The ACR Appropriateness Criteria rate it usually appropriate in one of eight variants only. It is not an answer for a sub-centimetre lesion, and per-lesion sensitivity for colorectal liver metastases, 81.4%, is no better than MRI at 80.3%.
approvals.audit: PET-CT ordered for liver characterisation, by lesion size and risk category.

approvals.q: What is the standing rule on biopsying a lesion that is going to be resected, and does it apply identically across diseases?
approvals.why: This page presents one rule, but the evidence ranges from a 19% needle-track rate in 90 patients biopsied before referral — with a 61%-against-26% imbalance in synchronous disease and no valid adjustment — to a 2.7% (1.8-4.0) pooled seeding rate in hepatocellular carcinoma whose largest prospective contributing study found zero events, to a six-patient series in perihilar disease. Whether to keep one rule or three is a genuine decision.
approvals.audit: Biopsies performed on subsequently resected lesions; biopsies in patients with resectable colorectal liver metastases; needle-track recurrences.

approvals.q: What surveillance interval, if any, applies to regenerative and focal-nodular-hyperplasia-like nodules in a liver with a vascular disorder?
approvals.why: LI-RADS excludes these livers and EASL's benign-tumour guideline withdraws its no-follow-up rule for this setting without supplying an interval. There is no guideline answer and the page should not invent one silently.
approvals.audit: Interval set, adherence, and the proportion of these nodules that changed category or required tissue.

approvals.q: What constitutes the completed search for an occult cancer after a cryptogenic pyogenic liver abscess, and does it include colonoscopy in every case?
approvals.why: The national cohort found standardised incidence ratios of 34.58 for biliary tract cancer and 5.27 for colorectal cancer, but the highest ratios all fell within the first 90 days, which means most of the signal is prevalent disease found during the index admission rather than incident disease. That supports completing a search now; it does not define the search.
approvals.audit: Searches completed during the index admission; cancers found, and when.

approvals.q: Who owns a follow-up interval recommended in a radiology report, and how is the loop closed?
approvals.why: Not an evidence question. An interval with no owner is the pathway's commonest failure, and the local CPG already requires an owner and due date for any conditional disposition.
approvals.audit: Named owner recorded at the time the interval was set; interval adherence.

approvals.q: What constitutes an adequate index study for the purpose of discharging a lesion?
approvals.why: Every benign-feature rule on this page assumes adequate phases and adequate dose. The ACR white paper warns that dose-reduced studies make small lesions hard to assess but does not define adequacy, and the local CPG requires the team to document inadequacy without saying what it is.
approvals.audit: Cases in which a discharge decision was reversed on a subsequent adequate study.

approvals.q: Who owns the update check on the ACR incidental liver white paper, the LI-RADS versions, and the EASL and AASLD guidance, and on what cycle?
approvals.why: The liver white paper is from 2017 with no revision published since and no update interval stated, CT/MRI LI-RADS has been at v2018 since August 2018 with only treatment-response and ultrasound-surveillance modules updated to v2024, CEUS LI-RADS remains at v2017, the ACR Appropriateness Criteria liver topic dates from 2020 and closed its evidence base before both the CEUS LI-RADS validation work and the 2022 individual-patient-data meta-analysis, and the EASL benign-tumour guideline of 2016 predates the molecular adenoma classification now in use. A page built on sources that are not being revised on a predictable schedule needs a named owner watching for the next one.
approvals.audit: Named owner plus edition and date for each source, with an agreed review cycle.

approvals.q: Which prevalence figure, if any, may be quoted to a patient or written into a report as the probability that an incidental liver lesion is benign?
approvals.why: The four figures in circulation are not comparable and none of them answers the question. Karhunen's 52% is a targeted-autopsy rate in 95 Finnish men, half of it lesions of 1.3 mm; Jones's 17% is a per-examination rate in cancer-surveillance CT; Schwartz's 12.7% is a report-mention rate conditioned on surviving to a second scan; Kaltenbach's 15.1% counts five benign findings and never counted a malignancy. The ACR's 'up to 30% over 40' has nineteen references and no pooled estimate behind it. The group has to decide whether the programme quotes a number at all, and if so which population it names alongside it.
approvals.audit: Reports and patient letters quoting a single prevalence figure without its denominator.

approvals.q: May a LI-RADS category assigned on one modality be acted on, or carried forward, when the comparison study was a different modality?
approvals.why: Intermodality agreement is kappa 0.33-0.39 between CT and MRI and 0.22 between MRI and CEUS, with CT tending to undercategorise, and category agreement between two readers on the same CEUS study is only kappa 0.30-0.39. If the category determines management then management depends in part on which scanner the patient entered and who read it. The LI-RADS authors state this and do not resolve it.
approvals.audit: Cases in which the category changed between modalities or between readers, and whether management changed with it.

approvals.q: In which patients may contrast-enhanced ultrasound be used as the resolving test for a CT- or MRI-indeterminate observation, rather than as a first-line characterising test?
approvals.why: The only prospective evidence is a sub-analysis of 75 observations in 68 patients who were 97.1% cirrhotic, with readers who could see the prior CT or MRI, a reference standard that was follow-up CT or MRI in 72% of cases, predictive values resting on 7, 7, 6 and 1 observations, and 74% of LR-3 observations still indeterminate afterwards. The WFUMB guideline separately makes its only level-1 strong recommendation for CEUS first-line in a non-cirrhotic liver without suspected malignancy — the opposite population — on a block citation with no pooled estimate. The two positions need reconciling locally, and the agent's manufacturer part-funded the first.
approvals.audit: CEUS performed after an indeterminate CT or MRI, by risk category, and whether it changed the disposition.

approvals.q: Which route is used when tissue is needed from a liver lesion — percutaneous core, endoscopic ultrasound-guided fine-needle biopsy, or transjugular — and who decides?
approvals.why: No source this page uses reports comparable harm figures for the three routes. Percutaneous morbidity is quoted as 0.5% by the 2017 ACR paper and 2.0-4.8% by the same committee in 2010; AASLD gives severe bleeding at 1 in 2,500 to 1 in 10,000 for diffuse non-focal disease and notes the risk may be higher for a malignant lesion; the pooled liver adverse-event rate for endoscopic ultrasound-guided fine-needle biopsy is 14.0% (7.7-24.0) on 133 patients, with a death in the numerator that the paper's conclusion denies. Cirrhosis and a hypervascular tumour are named as risk factors in the same review that concedes it could not analyse either.
approvals.audit: Route recorded for every liver biopsy, with complications by route and by platelet count, coagulation and ascites status.

approvals.q: Which edition of the EASL vascular-liver guidance governs this pathway, and who obtains and reads the 2026 edition?
approvals.why: Everything on this page about nodules in a vascular liver is sourced to the 2015 guideline, which was built on one 2012 conference agenda with a PubMed-only search and committee opinion where evidence was absent, and which has been superseded. The 2026 edition was not obtained for this revision, so the vascular arm of gate 0 and the alternative column of gate 5 are provisional.
approvals.audit: Named owner, edition and date on file; cases managed under the superseded edition after the new one became available.

approvals.q: Does an incidentally discovered nodular non-cirrhotic liver, or incidentally reported nodular regenerative hyperplasia, trigger a porto-sinusoidal vascular disorder workup — and does that include a biopsy?
approvals.why: The 2026 multisociety consensus makes nodular regenerative hyperplasia a major histological criterion for the disorder and makes liver biopsy mandatory for the diagnosis, with adequacy set at 15 mm including one 10 mm fragment. But its criteria were derived in 88 European patients who all had portal hypertension while the definition permits diagnosis without it, a major criterion needs only 10% sensitivity, its diagnostic score was fitted to expert votes on 36 hypothetical scenarios and reproduced them by construction, and it offers no guidance at all on incidentally detected nodularity and no risk-benefit analysis for biopsying an asymptomatic patient. Whether the programme adopts an unvalidated score and a mandatory biopsy for an incidental finding is a decision, not a reading of the guideline.
approvals.audit: Patients with incidental nodularity or reported nodular regenerative hyperplasia, the workup performed, biopsies done and diagnoses reached.

provenance: Revised on 7 October 2026 after a full-text read of this pathway's depot: thirty papers read in full and abstracted, each with the authors' own stated limitations and an independent critique. The revision corrected or qualified forty-one evidence strings, rewrote the prevalence quick reference so that every figure carries its denominator, downgraded fifteen evidence grades, added five papers, and roughly doubled the honest section. No recommendation was removed; the page's positions stand, and what changed is how well supported they are said to be. Built originally as a first draft from the UTHealth Houston / Memorial Hermann Transplant Oncology Master Workup and Staging CPG — a programme companion document that is itself a draft for institutional review, with its companion protocol set reviewed 20 July 2026 — together with the published imaging and benign-liver literature. The imaging backbone is the ACR Incidental Findings Committee white paper on incidental liver lesions on CT (Gore 2017, still the current version; no liver revision has been published and the ACR lists no liver topic under development), its 2010 predecessor, ACR CT/MRI LI-RADS v2018 Core and CEUS LI-RADS v2017 (both checked 6 October 2026 and both still the current diagnostic versions; the 2024 LI-RADS releases cover treatment response and ultrasound surveillance only), and the ACR Appropriateness Criteria topic Liver Lesion-Initial Characterization of 2020, now read in full as Chernyak 2020. The benign entities follow the EASL Clinical Practice Guidelines on the management of benign liver tumours of 2016 — still the last full guideline for haemangioma and focal nodular hyperplasia — with the subsequent literature used to say where that document has been overtaken, principally the 2022 subtype-stratified meta-analysis of hepatobiliary-phase signal. The LI-RADS evidence now includes the 2022 individual-patient-data meta-analysis of the major features and the prospective CEUS LI-RADS validation sub-analysis of 2024. Nodules in vascular livers are governed by the EASL vascular-liver guidance of 2015 together with the 2026 multisociety consensus on porto-sinusoidal vascular disorder. The at-risk fork and the diagnostic criteria for hepatocellular carcinoma follow the EASL hepatocellular carcinoma guideline of 2025 and the AASLD practice guidance of 2023. Say plainly what was not read. Six sources on this page are still cited from abstract or guideline text only and were not in the full-text depot: the EASL hepatocellular carcinoma guideline 2025 (PMID 39690085), the AASLD practice guidance 2023 (37199193), the three DEGUM contrast-enhanced ultrasound papers (19241506, 20740399, 25812115), the perihilar fine-needle aspiration series (21492336) and the fatty-liver imaging review (17102041). Every figure attributed to those sources is at the first draft's evidentiary standard. Two documents named in the gap scan were sought and not obtained, and are not cited here as read: the 2026 EASL guideline on vascular diseases of the liver, which supersedes the 2015 edition this page quotes and makes the whole of the vascular arm provisional, and the CAMINO study. Every PMID was verified against PubMed on 6 October 2026. This is a triage page: it starts at the scan and ends by routing to the HCC, iCCA, cHCC-CCA, CRLM, NELM or HCA pathway, and it makes no treatment recommendation beyond drainage of an abscess and the decision not to intervene on a lesion it resolves. Plainly: there is no ratified roadmap behind this page. No institutional decision has been taken on any threshold, interval or discharge rule in it except where the local CPG is quoted directly, every one of the sixteen ratification items in the approvals list is genuinely open, and every numeric criterion must be verified against the current source before use.
